About this edition

This is the second edition of the MYP 3 mathematics coursebook. It was rebuilt from the pre-rewrite MYP 3 audit, which recorded the chapter scope, the key and related concepts, the global contexts and the inquiry questions of the earlier edition, and identified where the teaching had to be strengthened.

The edition keeps that chapter scope and the visual identity of the collection, and rebuilds the teaching sequence around inquiry: engagement, inquiry questions, investigation, observation, mathematical conclusion, formal development, worked examples, extensive visual practice, and application, assessment and reflection.

Year 3 asks more of Criterion C than Year 2: reasoning must now be organised into a logical structure, and Criterion B moves from recognising and verifying a pattern to justifying a generalisation. The chapters train both explicitly.

All classroom data sets are simulated and are labelled as such. Real data would require provenance, so no claim in this book rests on unverified statistics.

No publisher, ISBN, print specification or commercial print-readiness claim is made in this file. The book is produced as an A4 review copy: fonts are embedded, pagination is continuous and every page has been checked for overflow.

MYP 3 · Student coursebook

How to use this book

Each chapter follows the same sequence, so you always know what is coming next. The sequence is deliberate: you investigate before you are told the rule, because a rule you have discovered is a rule you can defend — and defending it is what Year 3 asks of you.

The chapter sequence

  1. Engagement. A short situation that raises the question the chapter will answer.
  2. Inquiry questions. Factual, conceptual and debatable questions that frame the chapter.
  3. Investigation. A task you complete before the formal teaching: record evidence in a table and look for a pattern.
  4. Observation and discovery. What you noticed, stated in your own words and compared with a partner.
  5. Mathematical conclusion. The rule that the evidence supports, written as a general statement you can justify.
  6. Formal development. The explanation, definitions and notation, with the reasoning made explicit.
  7. Worked examples. Problem, visual representation, mathematical reasoning, step-by-step solution, final answer and interpretation.
  8. Practice. Separated into Criterion A, B, C and D practice, with visual representations throughout.
  9. Application, assessment and reflection. Real-context tasks, criterion-based assessment practice, and a reflection that returns to the statement of inquiry.

How to use this book

The four MYP mathematics criteria

A · Knowing and understanding

Apply knowledge to familiar and unfamiliar problems, and check results.

B · Investigating patterns

Investigate relationships, describe patterns, formulate a conjecture, test it and justify the generalisation — at Year 3 level a justification is a logical argument, not a list of examples.

C · Communicating

Use correct mathematical language, notation and complete representations, and organise reasoning into a coherent structure that a reader can follow.

D · Applying mathematics in real-life contexts

Apply mathematics to authentic situations, identify relevant information, and comment on the accuracy and sense of the result.

Working with this book

  • Practice is separated by criterion so that you can see which skill a task is training. Criterion B practice is additional genuine pattern investigation, not a repeat of the teaching.
  • Visuals are part of the mathematics. Where a task supplies a diagram, grid, table, number line or model, use it; where it asks you to sketch, your drawing is part of the answer.
  • Answers and student-facing reasoning are collected at the back of the book, with a formula bank, a glossary and references.
  • Every chapter ends with project connections: a Service as Action opportunity, a Community Project connection and a Personal Project connection for MYP 5.
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookIntroduction
MYP 3 · Student coursebook

MYP mathematics and this coursebook

The IB Middle Years Programme asks students to inquire into concepts through global contexts, to develop approaches to learning (ATL) skills, and to act on what they learn through service as action. In mathematics this means more than practising procedures: students investigate patterns, justify generalisations, communicate with precise language and apply mathematics to situations that matter to them.

MYP mathematics is organised into four branches — number, algebra, geometry and trigonometry, and statistics and probability — and the programme recommends at least 50 hours of teaching per subject each year. This coursebook covers the Year 3 content of those branches across ten chapters, grouped into four parts.

Year 3 is the level at which justification becomes central. A pattern spotted in three cases is a conjecture; a pattern shown to follow from something already established is a theorem. The chapters in this book keep that distinction visible, and the practice under each criterion says which kind of thinking it is training.

Assessment in MYP mathematics uses four equally weighted criteria, each with a maximum of 8: A knowing and understanding, B investigating patterns, C communicating, and D applying mathematics in real-life contexts. This book trains each criterion explicitly, and says so on the page where the training happens.

MYP mathematics and this coursebook

Projects, service and action

Service as Action

Each chapter includes a service opportunity with a community need, a mathematical connection, a proposed action, an expected impact and a student reflection. Completing an exercise is not service: service requires action that benefits others and reflection on that action.

Community Project

MYP students completing the programme in Year 3 or Year 4 complete a community project. Each chapter offers a student-led project idea with a research question, the mathematics involved, an action or outcome, beneficiaries and evidence. Follow your school's requirements and supervision.

Personal Project (MYP 5)

Students completing MYP in Year 5 complete a personal project. Each chapter offers an adaptable MYP 5-oriented extension with a personal interest, a learning goal, a product, the mathematics involved, a process and evidence. It is deliberately different from the community project and from service as action.

What this book does not claim

  • Programme requirements quoted here follow the official IB MYP curriculum, mathematics and projects pages and the MYP general regulations. Everything else — the chapter sequence, the investigations, the practice sets and the project ideas — is author-designed material built to serve those requirements, and is not an IB publication.
  • No ISBN, publisher, imprint or print specification is claimed. The file is an A4 review copy with embedded fonts and continuous pagination, produced for proofing and classroom review rather than for commercial print production.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookChapter 1 · The real number system
Chapter 1 · Part I · Number and abstraction
01

The real number system

Every fraction is a terminating or a recurring decimal. The converse is false, and the numbers that escape the fractions are the ones that make the number line continuous.

Engage

A surveyor measures a plot of land and records 12.7 m, then 12.73 m, then 12.732 m. Each measurement is better, and none of them is the true length. What kind of number is the true length?

Framing the inquiry

Key concept: Form
Related concepts: Quantity · Equivalence
Global context: Orientation in space and time
Global context exploration: Natural and human landscapes and resources

Statement of inquiry: The form of the real number system, and the equivalence between fractions, terminating decimals and recurring decimals, allow any position between two reference points to be described exactly, while the logic of proof shows that some positions on that line can never be written as a fraction.

Questions to guide us

  • Factual: Which numbers can be written as fractions, and what are the only two decimal forms a fraction can take?
  • Conceptual: Why can every fraction be written as a terminating or recurring decimal, and why is the converse false?
  • Debatable: When a land boundary is recorded to the nearest centimetre, is the recorded number the same number as the true distance, and does the difference matter?
ATL · Critical thinking. In order for a student to evaluate a claim about all numbers, students must test the claim on several cases, search for a counterexample, and then decide whether a counterexample disproves the claim or widens the definition.
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.1
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.1

Rational numbers and decimal form

Inquiry question

How can every fraction be written as a decimal, and what are the only two forms that decimal can take?

Your task

Take the fractions 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/6, 1/7, 1/8, 1/9, 1/11 and 1/12. Divide each one out to at least eight decimal places and record whether the decimal stops, repeats a single digit, or repeats a block of several digits. Then look at the denominators.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.1
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.1

Rational numbers and decimal form

What do you notice?
  • Every fraction gave either a stopping decimal or a repeating one — never a decimal that wandered without repeating.
  • The denominators that stop are built only from the primes 2 and 5.
  • 1/7 repeats a block of six digits, and 7 − 1 = 6, which is not a coincidence.
Observation. Long division of a fraction can only leave a limited number of remainders, so the decimal must stop or repeat.
Mathematical conclusion

Every fraction can be written as a decimal, and that decimal is either terminating or recurring — a terminating decimal exactly when the denominator in simplest form has no prime factor other than 2 or 5.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook1.1 · Rational numbers and decimal form
Chapter 1 · 1.1

Rational numbers and decimal form

A rational number is any number that can be written as a/b where a and b are integers and b is not zero. Every integer is rational, because n = n/1.

Dividing the numerator by the denominator gives a decimal that either stops (terminating) or settles into a repeating block (recurring). Nothing else can happen: the remainders in a long division can only take b different values, so one of them must eventually repeat.

A terminating decimal is a fraction whose denominator has only the prime factors 2 and 5. A recurring decimal comes from any other denominator. This is why 3/8 terminates (8 = 2³) but 1/3 recurs.

A recurring decimal is converted back to a fraction by multiplying by a power of 10 and subtracting, which cancels the repeating block.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook1.1 · Worked example 1
Chapter 1 · 1.1 · Worked example 1

Rational numbers and decimal form

Worked example 1.1.1

Problem. Write 5/8 and 7/12 as decimals, and say which one terminates and why.

Mathematical reasoning. A decimal terminates exactly when the denominator in simplest form has no prime factor other than 2 or 5.

  1. 5/8: 8 = 2³, so 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625, which stops.
  2. 7/12: 12 = 2² × 3, and the factor 3 forces repetition.
  3. 7 ÷ 12 = 0.58333… = 0.58·3·, with the digit 3 repeating.

Final answer. 5/8 = 0.625 terminates; 7/12 = 0.58·3· recurs

Interpretation. The shape of the denominator decides the shape of the decimal, so the fraction form carries information the decimal form hides.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook1.1 · Worked example 2
Chapter 1 · 1.1 · Worked example 2

Rational numbers and decimal form

Worked example 1.1.2

Problem. Convert 0.4·5· back to a fraction.

Mathematical reasoning. Multiplying by a power of 10 shifts the repeating block, and subtracting removes it.

  1. Let x = 0.4555….
  2. 10x = 4.555…, and 100x = 45.555….
  3. 100x − 10x = 41, so 90x = 41.
  4. x = 41/90.

Final answer. 0.4·5· = 41/90

Interpretation. Every recurring decimal is rational, so the recurring bar is a claim about exactness, not about approximation.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.2
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.2

Irrational numbers and surds

Inquiry question

How can we show that a number exists on the number line that is not a fraction?

Your task

Draw a square of side 1 unit on grid paper and draw its diagonal. Use Pythagoras' theorem to find the length of the diagonal, then try to write that length as a fraction by testing denominators up to 20. Record how close each fraction gets.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.2
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.2

Irrational numbers and surds

What do you notice?
  • Every fraction lands close to the diagonal, and then misses it.
  • The errors get smaller, but they never reach zero.
  • The fractions that get close have larger and larger denominators.
Observation. Fractions can approach the diagonal as closely as we like without ever landing on it, so the length of the diagonal is not a fraction.
Mathematical conclusion

A proof by contradiction shows that no fraction can equal the diagonal of a unit square, so √2 exists on the number line and is irrational.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook1.2 · Irrational numbers and surds
Chapter 1 · 1.2

Irrational numbers and surds

An irrational number cannot be written as a/b for any integers a and b. Its decimal neither stops nor repeats, so it can never be written down in full — only named exactly (√2) or described (1.41421… to five decimal places).

The standard proof that √2 is irrational is a proof by contradiction: assume √2 = a/b in simplest form, square both sides, and show that a and b must both be even, which contradicts simplest form.

The parity argument is the engine of the proof. If a² = 2b² then a² is even, so a is even (because the square of an odd number is odd), so a = 2c, so 4c² = 2b², so b² is even, so b is even too.

A surd is an exact irrational root left in root form. Keeping √2 as √2 is exact; writing 1.41 is a rounded claim that will not survive being squared.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook1.2 · Worked example 1
Chapter 1 · 1.2 · Worked example 1

Irrational numbers and surds

Worked example 1.2.1

Problem. Prove that √2 is irrational.

Mathematical reasoning. Assume the opposite and derive a contradiction; a claim that leads to a contradiction must be false.

  1. Suppose √2 = a/b with a and b integers, b ≠\neq= 0, and the fraction in simplest form.
  2. Squaring gives 2 = a²/b², so a² = 2b².
  3. Then a² is even, so a is even: write a = 2c.
  4. Substituting: 4c² = 2b², so b² = 2c², so b² is even and b is even.
  5. Both a and b are even, contradicting simplest form.

Final answer. √2 is irrational

Interpretation. The contradiction came from the parity of a square, which is why no fraction can land exactly on √2.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook1.2 · Worked example 2
Chapter 1 · 1.2 · Worked example 2

Irrational numbers and surds

Worked example 1.2.2

Problem. Show that √3 is irrational, using the same structure of argument.

Mathematical reasoning. The same contradiction argument works with any prime under the root, because a prime dividing a square must divide the number itself.

  1. Suppose √3 = a/b in simplest form, so a² = 3b².
  2. Then 3 divides a², and since 3 is prime, 3 divides a: write a = 3c.
  3. Substituting gives 9c² = 3b², so b² = 3c², so 3 divides b.
  4. Both a and b are divisible by 3, contradicting simplest form.

Final answer. √3 is irrational

Interpretation. The argument transfers because the key fact — a prime dividing a square divides the root — holds for every prime.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.3
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.3

Order, absolute value and intervals

Inquiry question

How can every position on a line be described, and how does an interval decide which positions are included?

Your task

On a number line from −4 to 6, mark the intervals [−3, 1], (−3, 1], [−3, 1) and (−3, 1). For each one, list three numbers that belong to it and one number that does not. Then find two intervals whose union is [−4, 6] and whose intersection is a single number.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.3
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.3

Order, absolute value and intervals

What do you notice?
  • The four intervals differ only at the two endpoints.
  • Every interval contains infinitely many numbers, including irrationals.
  • The union of [−3, 1] and (1, 6] is [−3, 6], and their intersection is empty.
Observation. Square and round brackets record exactly which endpoints belong, and the union and intersection of intervals follow from that.
Mathematical conclusion

An interval is the set of numbers between two endpoints, and the bracket type decides inclusion: [a, b] includes both ends, (a, b) excludes both, and the mixed forms include exactly one.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook1.3 · Order, absolute value and intervals
Chapter 1 · 1.3

Order, absolute value and intervals

The real numbers fill the number line with no gaps: every point is a real number and every real number is a point. Quantity and order are therefore the same idea on a line: to compare two quantities is to compare their positions. Rational and irrational numbers are both dense — between any two there is another of each kind.

Absolute value measures distance from zero, so |x| = x when x ≥ 0 and |x| = −x when x < 0. It turns an ordering question into a distance question.

An interval is the set of numbers between two endpoints. Square brackets include the endpoint, round brackets exclude it, and mixing them gives a half-open interval.

Interval and set notation are two languages for the same object: [1, 4) is {x : 1 ≤ x < 4}, and the complement of that set is everything outside it.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook1.3 · Worked example 1
Chapter 1 · 1.3 · Worked example 1

Order, absolute value and intervals

Worked example 1.3.1

Problem. Solve |x − 3| < 2 and write the answer as an interval.

Mathematical reasoning. Absolute value measures distance, so |x − 3| < 2 means x is less than 2 units from 3.

  1. |x − 3| < 2 means −2 < x − 3 < 2.
  2. Add 3 to all three parts: 1 < x < 5.
  3. As an interval: (1, 5).

Final answer. x ∈\in∈ (1, 5)

Interpretation. Reading absolute value as distance turns an inequality into a picture of a line segment.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook1.3 · Worked example 2
Chapter 1 · 1.3 · Worked example 2

Order, absolute value and intervals

Worked example 1.3.2

Problem. Write {x : −3 ≤ x < 2} in interval notation, and describe its complement.

Mathematical reasoning. A square bracket keeps the endpoint and a round bracket removes it, so the notation records inclusion directly.

  1. −3 is included and 2 is excluded, so the interval is [−3, 2).
  2. The complement is everything outside: x < −3 or x ≥ 2.
  3. In interval notation: (−∞, −3) ∪\cup∪ [2, ∞).

Final answer. [−3, 2), with complement (−∞, −3) ∪\cup∪ [2, ∞)

Interpretation. The two notations disagree only about the endpoints, which is exactly the information a surveyor needs.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.4
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.4

Working with surds

Inquiry question

How can an irrational quantity be written exactly and still be calculated with?

Your task

Take the surds √8, √18, √50 and √72. Simplify each one, then add them in pairs. Then try to simplify √2 + √3 and record what happens. Finally, find a fraction with denominator 3 + √2 that has an integer denominator.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.4
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.4

Working with surds

What do you notice?
  • All four surds simplify to a multiple of √2.
  • 2√2 + 3√2 + 5√2 + 6√2 = 16√2, but only because they are all like surds.
  • √2 + √3 resists simplification because the surds are different.
  • Multiplying 1/(3 + √2) by (3 − √2)/(3 − √2) gives (3 − √2)/7.
Observation. Only like surds combine, and a surd denominator can always be cleared by multiplying by the conjugate.
Mathematical conclusion

A surd can be written exactly and calculated with by taking out square factors, collecting like surds and rationalising with a conjugate — and the simplified form is unique.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook1.4 · Working with surds
Chapter 1 · 1.4

Working with surds

Surds obey the same rules as powers with fractional indices: √a × √b = √(ab), and √a ÷ √b = √(a/b) for non-negative a and b.

Simplifying a surd means taking out the largest square factor: √72 = √(36 × 2) = 6√2. The simplified form is unique, which makes it a good form for comparing.

Rationalising a denominator replaces a surd in a denominator by an integer, by multiplying top and bottom by a conjugate. (1 + √2)(1 − √2) = 1 − 2 = −1, so the surd disappears.

Adding surds needs like surds: 3√2 + 5√2 = 8√2, but 3√2 + 5√3 cannot be simplified. Treating √2 as if it were √3 is the standard error.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook1.4 · Worked example 1
Chapter 1 · 1.4 · Worked example 1

Working with surds

Worked example 1.4.1

Problem. Simplify √200 and rationalise 6/√3.

Mathematical reasoning. Simplifying removes square factors, and multiplying by a conjugate clears a surd from a denominator without changing the value.

  1. √200 = √(100 × 2) = 10√2.
  2. 6/√3 = (6 × √3)/(√3 × √3) = 6√3/3.
  3. 6√3/3 = 2√3.

Final answer. √200 = 10√2 and 6/√3 = 2√3

Interpretation. Both answers are exact; writing 1.732… would lose the ability to check the work by squaring.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook1.4 · Worked example 2
Chapter 1 · 1.4 · Worked example 2

Working with surds

Worked example 1.4.2

Problem. Show that (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 1, and use it to rationalise 5/(2 + √3).

Mathematical reasoning. The product of a conjugate pair is rational, so multiplying by the conjugate is a legitimate way to clear a surd denominator.

  1. (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 2√3 + 2√3 − 3 = 1.
  2. 5/(2 + √3) = 5(2 − √3)/((2 + √3)(2 − √3)).
  3. = 5(2 − √3)/1 = 10 − 5√3.

Final answer. 5/(2 + √3) = 10 − 5√3

Interpretation. The conjugate works because the cross terms cancel, leaving only rational numbers.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.5
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.5

Sets, logic and proof

Inquiry question

How can a claim about all numbers be proved rather than tested?

Your task

Test four claims about numbers. For each one, either find a counterexample or write down why you believe it is true for every case: (1) the sum of two rational numbers is rational; (2) the sum of two irrational numbers is irrational; (3) a non-zero rational number times an irrational number is irrational; (4) there is a rational number between any two rational numbers.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.5
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.5

Sets, logic and proof

What do you notice?
  • Two claims were destroyed by a single counterexample each.
  • Two claims survived because an argument covered every case.
  • The average of two numbers always lies between them, which is why the rationals are dense.
Observation. Examples can disprove a universal claim but never prove one; proving requires an argument that covers every case.
Mathematical conclusion

A universal claim is proved by an argument that works for all cases and disproved by one counterexample, which is why proof and counterexample are complementary tools.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook1.5 · Sets, logic and proof
Chapter 1 · 1.5

Sets, logic and proof

A set is a collection of objects, described by listing its elements or by a rule. The universal set is everything under discussion, and the complement of A is everything in the universal set that is not in A.

Union gathers what is in either set; intersection keeps only what is in both. These two operations behave like 'or' and 'and' in logic, and Venn diagrams make the difference visible.

A universal claim ('every fraction has a recurring or terminating decimal') cannot be proved by examples. It needs an argument that works for all cases, and a single counterexample destroys it.

Proof by contradiction assumes the claim is false and derives an impossible consequence. It is the tool that proves √2 is irrational, and it is used again in Chapter 7 to prove Pythagoras-related results.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook1.5 · Worked example 1
Chapter 1 · 1.5 · Worked example 1

Sets, logic and proof

Worked example 1.5.1

Problem. A = {x : x is a factor of 12} and B = {x : x is a factor of 18}. List A ∪\cup∪ B and A ∩\cap∩ B.

Mathematical reasoning. Union collects everything in either set; intersection keeps only the common elements.

  1. A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12} and B = {1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18}.
  2. A ∪\cup∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18}.
  3. A ∩\cap∩ B = {1, 2, 3, 6}.

Final answer. A ∪\cup∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18}; A ∩\cap∩ B = {1, 2, 3, 6}

Interpretation. The intersection is the common structure the two sets share, which is why it is the useful part for comparing.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook1.5 · Worked example 2
Chapter 1 · 1.5 · Worked example 2

Sets, logic and proof

Worked example 1.5.2

Problem. Show that the claim 'the product of two irrational numbers is irrational' is false.

Mathematical reasoning. A universal claim fails if a single case contradicts it, so a counterexample is a complete refutation.

  1. The claim says: for all irrational a and b, ab is irrational.
  2. Take a = √2 and b = √2. Both are irrational.
  3. ab = √2 × √2 = 2, which is rational.
  4. So the claim is false.

Final answer. False — √2 × √2 = 2

Interpretation. Finding one counterexample is faster than testing many cases, and it is decisive.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookChapter review
Chapter 1 · Review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • A rational number is a fraction of integers; its decimal stops or recurs.
  • A decimal terminates exactly when the denominator has no prime factor but 2 and 5.
  • An irrational number cannot be written as a fraction; √2 is proved irrational by contradiction.
  • Absolute value measures distance from zero, so it turns order into distance.
  • An interval records which endpoints are included, using square and round brackets.
  • Surds are simplified by taking out square factors and rationalised by multiplying by a conjugate.
  • A universal claim is proved by an argument for all cases, or disproved by one counterexample.

Vocabulary

rational · irrational · terminating decimal · recurring decimal · surd · absolute value · interval · union · intersection · complement · proof by contradiction · counterexample · conjugate

Statement of inquiry

The form of the real number system, and the equivalence between fractions, terminating decimals and recurring decimals, allow any position between two reference points to be described exactly, while the logic of proof shows that some positions on that line can never be written as a fraction.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookChapter 2 · Powers, roots and scientific notation
Chapter 2 · Part I · Number and abstraction
02

Powers, roots and scientific notation

Index form is a representation that carries the size of a quantity in its shape. The exponent laws are patterns in that shape, and they are what make large and small numbers calculable.

Engage

A drop of seawater contains about 10²² atoms. A red blood cell is about 10−5^{-5}−5 m wide. Writing these in full is impossible; writing them in index form is not, and the comparison becomes immediate.

Framing the inquiry

Key concept: Form
Related concepts: Quantity · Representation · Patterns
Global context: Scientific and technical innovation
Global context exploration: Precision, accuracy and measurement

Statement of inquiry: The form of a number written in index form, and the equivalence between index form and root form, allow any quantity to be represented compactly and compared across scales, while the pattern in the exponent laws makes those representations safe to manipulate.

Questions to guide us

  • Factual: What do the exponent laws say, and how do you write a root as a power?
  • Conceptual: Why does multiplying powers of the same base add the indices, and what does that reveal about the form of a number in index notation?
  • Debatable: When a measurement is reported to a certain number of significant figures, does the extra precision of a longer decimal make the claim more scientific?
ATL · Research. In order for a student to use an index law correctly in an unfamiliar problem, students must test the law on small cases, record where it breaks, and state the conditions under which the law holds.
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.1
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.1

Integer exponents and the exponent laws

Inquiry question

How can the pattern in repeated multiplication be written once, as a rule that works for every case?

Your task

Compute 2² × 2³, 2³ × 2⁴, 2⁵ × 2⁵ and 2² × 2⁵ both as products of factors and as single powers of 2. Then do the same for division, and for (2²)³ and (2³)². Record the pattern you see in the indices.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.1
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.1

Integer exponents and the exponent laws

What do you notice?
  • Multiplying adds the indices, and the reason is that the factors pile up.
  • Dividing subtracts them, because division removes factors.
  • A power of a power multiplies the indices, because each factor is itself a repeated multiplication.
  • 2⁵ ÷ 2⁵ must equal 1, and the pattern says 25−5^{5-5}5−5 = 2⁰, so 2⁰ = 1.
Observation. Each law is the same statement about counting factors, written in index form.
Mathematical conclusion

am^{m}m × an^{n}n = am+n^{m+n}m+n, am^{m}m ÷ an^{n}n = am−n^{m-n}m−n and (am^{m}m)n^{n}n = amn^{mn}mn, and these patterns are what force the definitions a⁰ = 1 and a−n^{-n}−n = 1/an^{n}n.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook2.1 · Integer exponents and the exponent laws
Chapter 2 · 2.1

Integer exponents and the exponent laws

An index records repeated multiplication: 2⁵ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2. The base is 2 and the index is 5, and the index is a count of factors, not a multiplier.

Multiplying powers of the same base adds the indices, because the factors simply accumulate: 2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷. Dividing subtracts them, because division removes factors.

A power of a power multiplies the indices, because each of the factors is itself a repeated multiplication: (2³)⁴ = 2¹².

The laws hold for every integer index once a⁰ = 1 and a−n^{-n}−n = 1/an^{n}n are defined. Those definitions are chosen so the patterns in the exponent laws continue without a break, and the same patterns extend to roots.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook2.1 · Worked example 1
Chapter 2 · 2.1 · Worked example 1

Integer exponents and the exponent laws

Worked example 2.1.1

Problem. Simplify (3x⁴)³ ÷ (9x²) and write the answer with positive indices.

Mathematical reasoning. The power law multiplies the indices inside the bracket, and the quotient law subtracts them, with the coefficients handled separately.

  1. (3x⁴)³ = 3³ × (x⁴)³ = 27x¹².
  2. 27x¹² ÷ 9x² = (27 ÷ 9) × x12−2^{12-2}12−2.
  3. = 3x¹⁰.

Final answer. 3x¹⁰

Interpretation. The coefficient and the variable part obey different laws, so keeping them separate avoids the commonest error.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook2.1 · Worked example 2
Chapter 2 · 2.1 · Worked example 2

Integer exponents and the exponent laws

Worked example 2.1.2

Problem. Evaluate 5−2^{-2}−2 × 5⁵ ÷ 5⁰.

Mathematical reasoning. Negative and zero indices are defined so that the same laws continue to work, so they can be used in the same calculation.

  1. 5−2^{-2}−2 × 5⁵ = 5−2+5^{-2+5}−2+5 = 5³.
  2. 5⁰ = 1 by definition.
  3. 5³ ÷ 1 = 125.

Final answer. 125

Interpretation. The definitions of a⁰ and a−n^{-n}−n are not arbitrary: they are exactly what the pattern in the laws requires.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.2
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.2

Roots and rational exponents

Inquiry question

How can a root be written as a power, and why are the two forms equivalent?

Your task

Take the numbers 4, 8, 27 and 32. Write each as a power of its smallest possible base, then write each root n^{n}n√a as a fractional index. Finally, test whether √(ab) = √a × √b holds for a = 9, b = 16 and for a = −9, b = 16, and record what you find.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.2
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.2

Roots and rational exponents

What do you notice?
  • Every root could be written as a fractional index.
  • √(9 × 16) = √144 = 12, and √9 × √16 = 3 × 4 = 12, so the law holds.
  • √(−9 × 16) is not a real number, so the law cannot be tested there.
  • Writing numbers as powers of the smallest base makes roots easy to see.
Observation. A root and a fractional index are two notations for the same operation, so the exponent laws apply to roots too.
Mathematical conclusion

n^{n}n√a = a^(1/n), so a^(m/n) = (n^{n}n√a)m^{m}m and the exponent laws extend to roots — for non-negative a when n is even.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook2.2 · Roots and rational exponents
Chapter 2 · 2.2

Roots and rational exponents

The nth root of a number is the value that, raised to the nth power, gives the number back: n^{n}n√a = a^(1/n). The two notations are equivalent because (a^(1/n))n^{n}n = a.

Writing roots as fractional indices lets the exponent laws apply to roots as well: √a × √b = a^(1/2) × b^(1/2) = (ab)^(1/2) = √(ab).

A rational index a^(m/n) means the nth root raised to the mth power, and the order of the two operations does not matter for non-negative a.

Negative indices give reciprocals, so a^(−1/2) = 1/√a. Keeping the sign separate from the fraction is what prevents sign errors.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook2.2 · Worked example 1
Chapter 2 · 2.2 · Worked example 1

Roots and rational exponents

Worked example 2.2.1

Problem. Write ³√(8x⁶) using index notation, then simplify.

Mathematical reasoning. The cube root is the power 1/3, and the power law multiplies indices, so 6 × 1/3 = 2.

  1. ³√(8x⁶) = (8x⁶)^(1/3).
  2. = 8^(1/3) × (x⁶)^(1/3).
  3. 8^(1/3) = 2 and (x⁶)^(1/3) = x^(6/3) = x².

Final answer. 2x²

Interpretation. Index form turns a root problem into an exponent problem, which is why it is the preferred form for manipulation.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook2.2 · Worked example 2
Chapter 2 · 2.2 · Worked example 2

Roots and rational exponents

Worked example 2.2.2

Problem. Simplify (16/81)^(−3/4).

Mathematical reasoning. A negative index inverts the fraction, and a fractional index takes a root before applying the power.

  1. (16/81)^(−3/4) = (81/16)^(3/4).
  2. (81/16)^(3/4) = (⁴√81 / ⁴√16)³ = (3/2)³.
  3. (3/2)³ = 27/8.

Final answer. 27/8

Interpretation. Doing the sign first, then the root, then the power keeps each step checkable.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.3
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.3

Scientific notation

Inquiry question

How can very large and very small quantities be written so that their size is visible at a glance?

Your task

Collect six quantities from science or geography at very different scales, write each in scientific notation, and order them from smallest to largest. Then multiply the smallest and the largest, and divide the largest by the smallest, without using a calculator for the exponents.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.3
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.3

Scientific notation

What do you notice?
  • Ordering by the exponent gives the correct order immediately.
  • The product of the smallest and largest had exponent −5 + 24 = 19.
  • The quotient had exponent 24 − (−5) = 29, so the two differ by 29 orders of magnitude.
  • Every coefficient stayed between 1 and 10, which is what makes the form readable.
Observation. The exponent carries the size of the quantity, so comparing, multiplying and dividing become operations on the exponents.
Mathematical conclusion

Scientific notation is a × 10n^{n}n with 1 ≤ a < 10, and multiplying or dividing such numbers adds or subtracts the exponents — which is the exponent law applied to a representation.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook2.3 · Scientific notation
Chapter 2 · 2.3

Scientific notation

Scientific notation writes a number as a × 10n^{n}n with 1 ≤ a < 10 and n an integer. The exponent counts how many places the decimal point has moved, so it carries the size of the quantity.

The form is a representation choice: 6 300 000 and 6.3 × 10⁶ are the same number, but only the second makes the order of magnitude visible.

Multiplying in scientific notation multiplies the coefficients and adds the exponents. Dividing does the reverse. This is the exponent law applied to a representation.

The form also prevents a common reporting error. A measurement written as 0.00042 m has hidden its scale; 4.2 × 10−4^{-4}−4 m has not.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook2.3 · Worked example 1
Chapter 2 · 2.3 · Worked example 1

Scientific notation

Worked example 2.3.1

Problem. Write 0.0000042 and 3 500 000 000 in scientific notation, then multiply them.

Mathematical reasoning. Move the decimal point until the coefficient lies between 1 and 10, then count the places moved to fix the exponent.

  1. 0.0000042: move the point 6 places right →\rightarrow→ 4.2 × 10−6^{-6}−6.
  2. 3 500 000 000: move the point 9 places left →\rightarrow→ 3.5 × 10⁹.
  3. Multiply: (4.2 × 3.5) × 10−6+9^{-6+9}−6+9 = 14.7 × 10³.
  4. Restore the form: 1.47 × 10⁴.

Final answer. 4.2 × 10−6^{-6}−6 and 3.5 × 10⁹; their product is 1.47 × 10⁴

Interpretation. The exponents add exactly as the index law says, and the coefficient is adjusted at the end to keep the form.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook2.3 · Worked example 2
Chapter 2 · 2.3 · Worked example 2

Scientific notation

Worked example 2.3.2

Problem. A red blood cell is 7.5 × 10−6^{-6}−6 m wide and a grain of sand is 2 × 10−4^{-4}−4 m wide. How many times wider is the grain?

Mathematical reasoning. Dividing divides the coefficients and subtracts the exponents, which gives the comparison directly.

  1. (2 × 10−4^{-4}−4) ÷ (7.5 × 10−6^{-6}−6) = (2 ÷ 7.5) × 10−4−(−6)^{-4-(-6)}−4−(−6).
  2. = 0.2666… × 10².
  3. = 2.666… × 10¹ ≈ 27.

Final answer. about 27 times wider

Interpretation. The subtraction of exponents gives the factor of 100 immediately, before any coefficient arithmetic.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.4
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.4

Orders of magnitude and estimation

Inquiry question

How can an order of magnitude decide whether a calculation is worth doing in detail?

Your task

Estimate each of these without a calculator, then check with one: the number of heartbeats in a year, the number of seconds in a school day, the number of grains of rice in a 1 kg bag, and the number of litres of water a class uses in a week. Record the order of magnitude of each estimate.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.4
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.4

Orders of magnitude and estimation

What do you notice?
  • Every estimate landed within a factor of 10 of the true value.
  • Estimating first made the calculator check meaningful.
  • The exponent of the estimate matched the exponent of the true value in three of the four cases.
  • The rice estimate was the least reliable, because the mass of one grain is a guess.
Observation. An order-of-magnitude estimate fixes the scale of an answer, which is enough to catch most errors.
Mathematical conclusion

The order of magnitude of a quantity is the power of 10 nearest to it, and estimating by orders of magnitude gives a value that is right in scale even when it is not right in detail.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook2.4 · Orders of magnitude and estimation
Chapter 2 · 2.4

Orders of magnitude and estimation

The order of magnitude of a quantity is the power of 10 nearest to it. Two quantities within a factor of 10 of each other share an order of magnitude.

Estimation by order of magnitude replaces every number by its leading digit times a power of 10, then works with the exponents. The answer is never exact, but it is always in the right scale.

An estimate is a check on a calculation. If a calculator answer is not within a factor of a few of the estimate, the calculation is wrong.

Rounding to one significant figure before calculating is the practical version of this idea, and it is the standard way to check a long computation.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook2.4 · Worked example 1
Chapter 2 · 2.4 · Worked example 1

Orders of magnitude and estimation

Worked example 2.4.1

Problem. Estimate 4.9 × 10⁷ × 6.1 × 10−3^{-3}−3 ÷ (2.0 × 10²) by order of magnitude, then compare with the calculator value.

Mathematical reasoning. Rounding each quantity to one significant figure keeps the exponent exact and makes the arithmetic mental.

  1. Rounded: (5 × 10⁷) × (6 × 10−3^{-3}−3) ÷ (2 × 10²).
  2. Coefficients: 5 × 6 ÷ 2 = 15.
  3. Exponents: 7 − 3 − 2 = 2.
  4. Estimate: 15 × 10² = 1.5 × 10³.
  5. Calculator: 1.4975 × 10³, so the estimate is close.

Final answer. about 1.5 × 10³, against a calculator value of 1.4975 × 10³

Interpretation. The estimate caught no error this time, but it would have caught a decimal point slip of two places.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook2.4 · Worked example 2
Chapter 2 · 2.4 · Worked example 2

Orders of magnitude and estimation

Worked example 2.4.2

Problem. A city of 2.4 × 10⁵ people uses 1.8 × 10¹⁰ litres of water a year. Estimate the use per person.

Mathematical reasoning. Dividing the total by the population gives the per-person value, and the exponents give the scale.

  1. (1.8 × 10¹⁰) ÷ (2.4 × 10⁵) = (1.8 ÷ 2.4) × 10⁵.
  2. 1.8 ÷ 2.4 = 0.75, so the answer is 0.75 × 10⁵.
  3. = 7.5 × 10⁴ litres per person per year.

Final answer. about 7.5 × 10⁴ litres per person per year

Interpretation. That is roughly 205 litres a day, which is a plausible order of magnitude for domestic use.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.5
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.5

Significant figures and precision

Inquiry question

How many digits of a measurement actually carry meaning?

Your task

Take the measurements 0.0042 m, 4.20 m, 42 m, 4200 m and 0.042 m. For each one, state the number of significant figures and the interval of possible true values. Then multiply 4.2 by 3.65 and decide how many digits of the answer are meaningful.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.5
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.5

Significant figures and precision

What do you notice?
  • Trailing zeros before a decimal point are ambiguous, which is why scientific notation is preferred.
  • 0.0042 and 0.042 both have two significant figures, even though one is ten times larger.
  • 4.20 has three significant figures and a narrower interval than 4.2.
  • 4.2 × 3.65 = 15.33, but only two of those digits are meaningful.
Observation. Significant figures count the digits that carry measured meaning, and the interval of true values gets narrower as the count rises.
Mathematical conclusion

The number of significant figures records the precision of a measurement, and a calculated result cannot honestly be reported to more significant figures than the least precise value that went into it.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook2.5 · Significant figures and precision
Chapter 2 · 2.5

Significant figures and precision

Significant figures are the digits of a measurement that carry meaning, counted from the first non-zero digit. Leading zeros are placeholders and are never significant; trailing zeros after a decimal point always are.

The number of significant figures records the precision of the instrument. A length of 3.6 m claims the nearest 10 cm; 3.60 m claims the nearest centimetre.

Rounding to a given number of significant figures follows the usual rule, but the count starts at the first non-zero digit, which is why 0.00452 to three significant figures is 0.00452 and to two is 0.0045.

When measurements are combined, the result cannot be more precise than the least precise input. Reporting more digits than the data supports is a false claim of precision.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook2.5 · Worked example 1
Chapter 2 · 2.5 · Worked example 1

Significant figures and precision

Worked example 2.5.1

Problem. Round 0.0040529 to three significant figures, and 604 512 to two.

Mathematical reasoning. The count begins at the first non-zero digit, so leading zeros are ignored and the decision digit is the one after the last significant figure.

  1. 0.0040529: the first non-zero digit is 4, so the three significant figures are 4, 0, 5 and the next digit is 2.
  2. 2 < 5, so 0.0040529 →\rightarrow→ 0.00405 to three significant figures.
  3. 604 512: the first two significant figures are 6 and 0, and the next digit is 4, which does not round up.
  4. So 604 512 →\rightarrow→ 600 000 = 6.0 × 10⁵ to two significant figures.

Final answer. 0.00405 and 6.0 × 10⁵

Interpretation. Writing 600 000 loses the claim about precision, so scientific notation is used to keep it.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook2.5 · Worked example 2
Chapter 2 · 2.5 · Worked example 2

Significant figures and precision

Worked example 2.5.2

Problem. A rectangle measures 4.2 m by 3.65 m. Find the area, reporting it to a sensible precision.

Mathematical reasoning. Multiplying measurements combines their errors, so the result is reported to the precision of the least precise input.

  1. Area = 4.2 × 3.65 = 15.33 m².
  2. The least precise side has two significant figures, so report to two.
  3. 15.33 m² →\rightarrow→ 15 m² to two significant figures.

Final answer. 15 m² (to two significant figures)

Interpretation. Reporting 15.33 m² would claim a precision that neither measurement supports.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookChapter review
Chapter 2 · Review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • An index counts repeated multiplication, so multiplying powers adds indices.
  • a⁰ = 1 and a−n^{-n}−n = 1/an^{n}n are defined so that the exponent laws continue without a break.
  • A root is a fractional index: n^{n}n√a = a^(1/n).
  • Scientific notation a × 10n^{n}n with 1 ≤ a < 10 makes the scale of a quantity visible.
  • Multiplying or dividing in scientific notation adds or subtracts the exponents.
  • The order of magnitude of a quantity is the nearest power of 10.
  • Significant figures record precision, counted from the first non-zero digit.

Vocabulary

index · base · exponent law · zero index · negative index · fractional index · scientific notation · order of magnitude · significant figure · precision

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookChapter 3 · Functions, expressions and algebraic reasoning
Chapter 3 · Part II · Algebra and models
03

Functions, expressions and algebraic reasoning

A letter stands for a quantity that changes. A function is the relationship that gives each input one output, and equivalent forms of its rule reveal different things about that relationship.

Engage

A phone plan costs 12 dollars a month plus 0.05 dollars a minute. For one month the bill depends entirely on the number of minutes used. What is the relationship, and how can it be written once for every month?

Framing the inquiry

Key concept: Relationships
Related concepts: Generalisation · Equivalence
Global context: Identities and relationships
Global context exploration: Relationships and communities

Statement of inquiry: The relationship between two quantities can be generalised as a function, and the equivalence of the different algebraic forms of that relationship allows it to be rearranged, compared and used to predict.

Questions to guide us

  • Factual: What is a function, what are its domain and range, and how do you expand and factorise a quadratic expression?
  • Conceptual: Why do equivalent forms of the same expression reveal different information about the relationship they describe?
  • Debatable: Is a formula that has been rearranged a different formula, or the same formula in a different form — and does the difference matter?
ATL · Thinking. In order for a student to select an algebraic strategy for an unfamiliar expression, students must identify which form the problem is already in, decide which equivalent form the answer needs, and justify the choice.
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.1
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.1

Variables, expressions and substitution

Inquiry question

How can a changing quantity be represented by a letter, and what does substitution actually do?

Your task

A pattern of tiles has 1 tile in position 1, 4 in position 2, 7 in position 3 and 10 in position 4. Write the number of tiles as an expression in the position number n, then test it for n = 10 and n = 100. Then find a second, different expression that gives the same values.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.1
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.1

Variables, expressions and substitution

What do you notice?
  • The number of tiles rises by 3 each time, so the expression contains 3n.
  • Subtracting 2 makes the expression work from position 1 rather than position 0.
  • The expression 1 + 3(n − 1) gives the same values, and it expands to 3n − 2.
  • Both forms predict the same number of tiles at any position.
Observation. A pattern that grows by a constant amount is described by a linear expression, and several equivalent expressions can describe it.
Mathematical conclusion

A generalisation of a growing pattern is an expression that works for every position, and equivalent expressions are different forms of the same generalisation.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook3.1 · Variables, expressions and substitution
Chapter 3 · 3.1

Variables, expressions and substitution

A variable is a letter standing for a number that can change. It is not an unknown to be found: it is a quantity that takes different values in different situations.

An expression is a recipe built from variables, numbers and operations. 3n + 5 is a recipe that takes a number n, triples it and adds 5. The order of operations fixes what the recipe does.

Substitution replaces a variable by a value and evaluates. It is the point at which a general relationship becomes a specific number.

Two expressions that give the same value for every substitution are equivalent. Testing a few values suggests equivalence but never proves it; expansion or factorisation proves it.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook3.1 · Worked example 1
Chapter 3 · 3.1 · Worked example 1

Variables, expressions and substitution

Worked example 3.1.1

Problem. A taxi charges 3.50 dollars plus 1.80 dollars per kilometre. Write the cost as an expression and find the cost of a 12 km trip.

Mathematical reasoning. The cost has a fixed part and a variable part, so the expression is a linear recipe in the number of kilometres.

  1. Let k be the number of kilometres.
  2. Cost = 3.50 + 1.80k.
  3. For k = 12: cost = 3.50 + 1.80 × 12 = 3.50 + 21.60.
  4. = 25.10 dollars.

Final answer. C = 3.50 + 1.80k; a 12 km trip costs 25.10 dollars

Interpretation. The expression works for every trip, not just this one, which is why it is worth writing.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook3.1 · Worked example 2
Chapter 3 · 3.1 · Worked example 2

Variables, expressions and substitution

Worked example 3.1.2

Problem. Show that 4(x + 3) and 4x + 12 are equivalent.

Mathematical reasoning. Expanding the bracket shows the two forms have the same value for every x, which is what equivalence means.

  1. 4(x + 3) means four copies of (x + 3).
  2. Four copies of x give 4x, and four copies of 3 give 12.
  3. So 4(x + 3) = 4x + 12.
  4. Check with x = 2: 4 × 5 = 20 and 8 + 12 = 20.

Final answer. 4(x + 3) = 4x + 12 for every value of x

Interpretation. The expanded form is easier to evaluate; the factorised form is easier to read. Equivalence lets us choose.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.2
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.2

Functions, domain and range

Inquiry question

How can a rule that gives each input exactly one output be represented, and what are its domain and range?

Your task

Take the rule 'multiply by 3, then subtract 1'. Build a table of values for inputs −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4, draw the mapping diagram, plot the points on a grid, and write the formula. Then change the rule to 'multiply by 3, then subtract a number of your choice' and repeat.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.2
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.2

Functions, domain and range

What do you notice?
  • The outputs rise by 3 each time the input rises by 1.
  • The points lie on a straight line, which is what a linear function looks like.
  • Changing the subtracted number moves the line up or down but does not change its steepness.
  • Every input gave exactly one output, so the rule is a function.
Observation. A rule that gives one output per input is a function, and a linear function gives outputs that change by a constant amount.
Mathematical conclusion

A function assigns exactly one output to each permitted input; its domain is the set of permitted inputs and its range the set of outputs, and both are choices the modeller makes.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook3.2 · Functions, domain and range
Chapter 3 · 3.2

Functions, domain and range

A function is a rule that gives exactly one output for each permitted input. The input is the independent variable and the output is the dependent variable.

Function notation f(x) names the rule and the input together: f(x) = 2x + 1 means the rule is double and add one. f(3) = 7 is the value of the function at x = 3.

The domain is the set of permitted inputs and the range is the set of outputs the rule can produce. The domain is a modelling choice, not a mathematical fact: a rule can be defined for all real numbers but only make sense for positive ones.

A function can be represented as a mapping diagram, a table of values, a graph or a formula. The four representations describe the same relationship, and each one answers a different question about it.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook3.2 · Worked example 1
Chapter 3 · 3.2 · Worked example 1

Functions, domain and range

Worked example 3.2.1

Problem. f(x) = 3x − 4. Find f(5), f(−2) and the value of x for which f(x) = 11.

Mathematical reasoning. Substitution evaluates the function, and solving a linear equation reverses it.

  1. f(5) = 3 × 5 − 4 = 11.
  2. f(−2) = 3 × (−2) − 4 = −10.
  3. 3x − 4 = 11 gives 3x = 15, so x = 5.

Final answer. f(5) = 11, f(−2) = −10, and f(x) = 11 when x = 5

Interpretation. Evaluating and solving are opposite operations on the same relationship.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook3.2 · Worked example 2
Chapter 3 · 3.2 · Worked example 2

Functions, domain and range

Worked example 3.2.2

Problem. A function is defined by the rule 'add 6 then divide by 2'. Write it as a formula, state a sensible domain, and find its range.

Mathematical reasoning. Translating a verbal rule into a formula makes the domain and range explicit.

  1. g(x) = (x + 6)/2.
  2. The formula is defined for every real x, so the domain is all real numbers.
  3. Every real y can be produced, because x = 2y − 6 is real for any y.
  4. So the range is also all real numbers.

Final answer. g(x) = (x + 6)/2, domain and range both all real numbers

Interpretation. A formula with no division by a variable and no root usually has the widest possible domain.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.3
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.3

Expanding and factorising

Inquiry question

How can equivalent forms of the same expression reveal different information about it?

Your task

Expand (x + 2)(x + 3), (x + 2)(x + 5), (x + 4)(x + 5) and (x + 2)(x − 3). Record the coefficient of x and the constant term in each case, and look for a pattern that connects them to the numbers inside the brackets.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.3
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.3

Expanding and factorising

What do you notice?
  • The coefficient of x is always the sum of the two numbers in the brackets.
  • The constant term is always the product of those two numbers.
  • A negative number in a bracket can give a negative coefficient or constant.
  • The pattern works in reverse, which is exactly what factorising does.
Observation. The expanded form of a product of two linear factors has coefficients that are the sum and product of the bracket numbers.
Mathematical conclusion

(x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab, so the expanded and factorised forms carry the same information in different arrangements, and factorising reads the pattern backwards.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook3.3 · Expanding and factorising
Chapter 3 · 3.3

Expanding and factorising

Expanding removes brackets by distributing: a(b + c) = ab + ac. It is the form that is easiest to evaluate and to collect like terms in.

Factorising is the reverse: it puts a common factor or a product of factors back in. The factorised form makes zeros and roots visible, which the expanded form hides.

Three products are worth knowing by sight: (x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab, (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² and a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b).

The difference of two squares is the most useful of the three, because it converts an addition into a product and is used again in Chapter 1 to rationalise a denominator.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook3.3 · Worked example 1
Chapter 3 · 3.3 · Worked example 1

Expanding and factorising

Worked example 3.3.1

Problem. Expand and simplify (x + 5)(x − 3), then factorise x² + 7x + 10.

Mathematical reasoning. Expanding distributes each term of one bracket over the other, and factorising looks for two numbers with the right sum and product.

  1. (x + 5)(x − 3) = x² − 3x + 5x − 15 = x² + 2x − 15.
  2. For x² + 7x + 10, find two numbers with product 10 and sum 7: 2 and 5.
  3. x² + 7x + 10 = (x + 2)(x + 5).

Final answer. (x + 5)(x − 3) = x² + 2x − 15 and x² + 7x + 10 = (x + 2)(x + 5)

Interpretation. The expanded form shows the shape of the quadratic; the factorised form shows where it equals zero.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook3.3 · Worked example 2
Chapter 3 · 3.3 · Worked example 2

Expanding and factorising

Worked example 3.3.2

Problem. Factorise 6x² + 9x completely, and use the result to solve 6x² + 9x = 0.

Mathematical reasoning. Taking out the highest common factor leaves a product, and a product equals zero only when one of its factors does.

  1. 6x² + 9x = 3x(2x + 3).
  2. So 3x(2x + 3) = 0.
  3. Either 3x = 0, giving x = 0, or 2x + 3 = 0, giving x = −3/2.

Final answer. 6x² + 9x = 3x(2x + 3); the solutions are x = 0 and x = −3/2

Interpretation. The factorised form solved an equation that the expanded form did not make easy.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.4
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.4

Rearranging formulas

Inquiry question

How can a formula be rewritten so that a different quantity is the subject?

Your task

Take the relationship d = 5t + 20, where d is a distance in metres and t is a time in seconds. Make t the subject, then find the time when d = 100. Then make a formula of your own with two letters and rearrange it the other way round.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.4
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.4

Rearranging formulas

What do you notice?
  • Rearranging did not change the relationship; it changed the question.
  • Every step was the same operation on both sides.
  • The constant 20 was removed by subtraction, which is the inverse of addition.
  • The rearranged form is easier when the distance is known and the time is not.
Observation. Rearranging applies inverse operations to both sides, so the relationship is preserved while the subject changes.
Mathematical conclusion

A formula can be rearranged into any subject by applying inverse operations to both sides in the reverse of the original order, and the rearranged formula is the same relationship answering a different question.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook3.4 · Rearranging formulas
Chapter 3 · 3.4

Rearranging formulas

Rearranging a formula means applying the same operation to both sides until the wanted letter is isolated. Every step must keep the statement true.

The operations are undone in the reverse of the order they were applied. To undo 'multiply by 3 then add 5', subtract 5 then divide by 3.

A formula rearranged into a different subject is not a different formula. It is the same relationship in a form that answers a different question.

Rearranging is the algebraic version of changing perspective: the same relationship, read from the other end.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook3.4 · Worked example 1
Chapter 3 · 3.4 · Worked example 1

Rearranging formulas

Worked example 3.4.1

Problem. The formula for the area of a trapezium is A = ½(a + b)h. Make h the subject.

Mathematical reasoning. The height is multiplied by (a + b) and by ½, so both are undone by reversing the order.

  1. A = ½(a + b)h.
  2. Multiply both sides by 2: 2A = (a + b)h.
  3. Divide both sides by (a + b): h = 2A/(a + b).

Final answer. h = 2A/(a + b)

Interpretation. The rearranged formula answers 'how high must it be' instead of 'what is the area', using the same relationship.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook3.4 · Worked example 2
Chapter 3 · 3.4 · Worked example 2

Rearranging formulas

Worked example 3.4.2

Problem. Make x the subject of y = (3x + 2)/(x − 1).

Mathematical reasoning. Clearing the denominator first, then collecting every term containing x, isolates the wanted letter by factorising.

  1. y(x − 1) = 3x + 2.
  2. yx − y = 3x + 2.
  3. yx − 3x = y + 2.
  4. x(y − 3) = y + 2.
  5. x = (y + 2)/(y − 3), for y ≠\neq= 3.

Final answer. x = (y + 2)/(y − 3)

Interpretation. The restriction y ≠\neq= 3 appears because x would then be undefined, which the original formula also hides.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.5
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.5

Sequences, patterns and generalisation

Inquiry question

How can a pattern in a sequence be written as a rule that works for any term?

Your task

Build three sequences from patterns of your own: one with a constant difference, one with a constant second difference, and one that is neither. For each, find the nth term and test it on two terms that were not in your original list.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.5
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.5

Sequences, patterns and generalisation

What do you notice?
  • The linear sequence had a constant difference of 4.
  • The quadratic sequence had a constant second difference of 2.
  • The third sequence had differences that grew by 1 each time, so it is not linear or quadratic.
  • Each nth term predicted a term that was not in the original list.
Observation. The pattern of first and second differences identifies the form of the nth term.
Mathematical conclusion

A generalisation is a rule that works for every position, and it is identified by the pattern of differences: a constant first difference gives a linear rule and a constant second difference gives a quadratic one.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook3.5 · Sequences, patterns and generalisation
Chapter 3 · 3.5

Sequences, patterns and generalisation

A sequence is an ordered list of numbers. The term-to-term rule says how to get from one term to the next; the position-to-term rule gives the term in any position directly.

A linear sequence has a constant difference, so its nth term is an + b. The difference gives a and substituting one term gives b.

A quadratic sequence has a constant second difference, so its nth term contains n². The second difference is twice the coefficient of n².

A generalisation is a claim about every term, not just the ones listed. Checking the first five terms supports a generalisation; it does not prove it, and a counterexample at the sixth term destroys it.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook3.5 · Worked example 1
Chapter 3 · 3.5 · Worked example 1

Sequences, patterns and generalisation

Worked example 3.5.1

Problem. Find the nth term of the sequence 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, … and use it to find the 50th term.

Mathematical reasoning. A constant difference means the rule is linear, so the nth term is an + b.

  1. The common difference is 4, so a = 4.
  2. The nth term is 4n + b.
  3. The first term is 7, so 4 × 1 + b = 7, giving b = 3.
  4. The nth term is 4n + 3, and the 50th term is 4 × 50 + 3 = 203.

Final answer. the nth term is 4n + 3; the 50th term is 203

Interpretation. The position-to-term rule gives any term without listing all the previous ones.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook3.5 · Worked example 2
Chapter 3 · 3.5 · Worked example 2

Sequences, patterns and generalisation

Worked example 3.5.2

Problem. The nth term of a sequence is n² − 2n. Find the first four terms and the second difference.

Mathematical reasoning. Substituting each position gives the terms, and the constant second difference confirms the quadratic form.

  1. n = 1: 1 − 2 = −1.
  2. n = 2: 4 − 4 = 0.
  3. n = 3: 9 − 6 = 3.
  4. n = 4: 16 − 8 = 8.
  5. First differences: 1, 3, 5; second difference: 2.

Final answer. the first four terms are −1, 0, 3, 8 and the second difference is 2

Interpretation. The second difference of 2 matches the coefficient of n², which is the signature of a quadratic.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookChapter review
Chapter 3 · Review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • A variable stands for a changing quantity, and an expression is a recipe built from variables.
  • A function gives exactly one output for each permitted input.
  • The domain is the set of permitted inputs and the range is the set of outputs.
  • Expanding and factorising produce equivalent forms of the same expression.
  • A difference of two squares factorises: a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b).
  • Rearranging applies inverse operations to both sides, preserving the relationship.
  • A constant first difference gives a linear rule; a constant second difference gives a quadratic rule.

Vocabulary

variable · expression · substitution · function · domain · range · function notation · expand · factorise · subject of a formula · sequence · nth term · generalisation
