MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookChapter review
Chapter 7 · Review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • Similar figures have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides.
  • For triangles, AA and SSS are sufficient similarity conditions.
  • Lengths scale by k and areas by k².
  • Pythagoras' theorem: a² + b² = c² for a right-angled triangle.
  • The converse tests whether a triangle is right-angled.
  • sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite/adjacent.
  • The angle of elevation equals the angle of depression by alternate angles.
  • Indirect measurement gives the height above eye level, so the eye height must be added.

Vocabulary

similar · scale factor · AA · SSS similarity · hypotenuse · leg · Pythagoras' theorem · sine · cosine · tangent · angle of elevation · angle of depression · indirect measurement · clinometer

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookChapter 8 · Three-dimensional solids and measurement
Chapter 8 · Part III · Shape, space and proof
08

Three-dimensional solids and measurement

A solid is described by its faces, edges and vertices. Its net gives the surface area, its cross-section gives the volume, and its density connects the two to the material it is made from.

Engage

A drinks manufacturer must choose between a cylindrical can and a rectangular carton of the same 330 ml capacity. Which uses less material? The answer is a comparison of surface areas, and the difference is not small.

Framing the inquiry

Key concept: Form
Related concepts: Measurement · Models
Global context: Globalisation and sustainability
Global context exploration: Human impact on the environment

Statement of inquiry: The form of a three-dimensional solid, and the measurement of its surface area and volume, allow the material it requires to be modelled, and those models show how design choices change the resources consumed.

Questions to guide us

  • Factual: What are the formulas for the surface area and volume of prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones and spheres?
  • Conceptual: Why does the volume of a cone equal one third of the cylinder that contains it, and how does the precision of a measurement limit the precision of a volume?
  • Debatable: Is a design that minimises material always the better environmental choice?
ATL · Self-management. In order for a student to manage a multi-step measurement task, students must select the correct formula, set out the substitution so each step can be checked, and review the units and the precision of the final result.
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.1
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.1

Solids, nets and views

Inquiry question

How can a three-dimensional solid be represented on a flat surface, and what does each representation preserve?

Your task

Build the net of a cuboid, a cylinder and a square-based pyramid from card. Fold each one and record the number of faces, edges and vertices, then check Euler's relation for the two polyhedra.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.1
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.1

Solids, nets and views

What do you notice?
  • Both polyhedra satisfied Euler's relation.
  • The cylinder has no vertices or edges in the polyhedral sense, so the relation does not apply.
  • The net of the cylinder is two circles and a rectangle whose length is the circumference.
  • The net of the pyramid is one square and four triangles.
Observation. A net flattens a solid without changing the shapes or areas of its faces, and Euler's relation checks the counts for any polyhedron.
Mathematical conclusion

A solid can be represented by its net, by its views and by a sketch, and the net is the representation that preserves the areas needed for surface area.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook8.1 · Solids, nets and views
Chapter 8 · 8.1

Solids, nets and views

A solid is described by its faces, edges and vertices. Euler's relation for a polyhedron is V − E + F = 2, which holds for every solid without a hole.

A net is a flat arrangement of the faces that folds into the solid. It preserves area and shape, which makes it the natural representation for surface area.

Front, side and plan views each show two dimensions and hide the third. Together they determine the solid, and each alone does not.

A solid can also be represented by a sketch in oblique or isometric projection. The projection is a drawing convention, not a mathematical property, and it distorts some measurements.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook8.1 · Worked example 1
Chapter 8 · 8.1 · Worked example 1

Solids, nets and views

Worked example 8.1.1

Problem. A cuboid has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. Check Euler's relation.

Mathematical reasoning. Euler's relation connects the counts of vertices, edges and faces for any polyhedron.

  1. V = 8, E = 12 and F = 6.
  2. V − E + F = 8 − 12 + 6.
  3. = 2.

Final answer. the relation holds

Interpretation. The relation is a check on a drawing: if it fails, the drawing is wrong.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook8.1 · Worked example 2
Chapter 8 · 8.1 · Worked example 2

Solids, nets and views

Worked example 8.1.2

Problem. Describe the net of a cube of side 3 cm and find its area.

Mathematical reasoning. The net of a cube is six squares, and its area is the surface area of the cube.

  1. A cube has 6 identical square faces.
  2. Each face has area 3 × 3 = 9 cm².
  3. Total area = 6 × 9 = 54 cm².

Final answer. six squares of area 9 cm² each, total 54 cm²

Interpretation. The net is the representation that turns a three-dimensional question into a flat one.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.2
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.2

Surface area of prisms and cylinders

Inquiry question

How can the surface area of a solid be found from its net?

Your task

Make the net of a cylinder from card, measure the rectangle and the two circles, and compute the total area. Then repeat for a cylinder of twice the radius and the same height, and compare the two surface areas.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.2
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.2

Surface area of prisms and cylinders

What do you notice?
  • Doubling the radius doubled the curved area but quadrupled the area of the ends.
  • The total area grew by a factor of about 2.55, not by 4.
  • The curved area depends on the radius linearly, while the ends depend on its square.
  • For the same volume, a wider and shorter cylinder uses less material than a narrow tall one.
Observation. The curved area scales with the radius and the height, while the ends scale with the square of the radius.
Mathematical conclusion

The surface area of a cylinder is 2πr² + 2πrh, read directly from a net of two circles and a rectangle of length 2πr and height h.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook8.2 · Surface area of prisms and cylinders
Chapter 8 · 8.2

Surface area of prisms and cylinders

The surface area of a prism is the sum of the areas of its faces: two congruent ends plus the lateral faces, which unfold into a rectangle.

For a cylinder, the two ends are circles of area πr² each and the curved surface unrolls into a rectangle of length 2πr and height h, so the curved area is 2πrh.

The total surface area of a cylinder is therefore 2πr² + 2πrh, and each term corresponds to a part of the net.

Reading the formula from the net is more reliable than memorising it, because the net shows where each term comes from.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook8.2 · Worked example 1
Chapter 8 · 8.2 · Worked example 1

Surface area of prisms and cylinders

Worked example 8.2.1

Problem. Find the surface area of a cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 10 cm.

Mathematical reasoning. The net is two circles and a rectangle whose length is the circumference.

  1. Area of the two ends = 2 × π × 3² = 18π cm².
  2. Curved area = 2π × 3 × 10 = 60π cm².
  3. Total = 18π + 60π = 78π cm².
  4. = 245.0 cm² to one decimal place.

Final answer. 78π cm², or about 245.0 cm²

Interpretation. The exact answer is left in terms of π, and the decimal is the reporting form.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook8.2 · Worked example 2
Chapter 8 · 8.2 · Worked example 2

Surface area of prisms and cylinders

Worked example 8.2.2

Problem. A rectangular prism measures 5 cm by 4 cm by 3 cm. Find its surface area.

Mathematical reasoning. A cuboid has three pairs of identical rectangular faces, so the total is twice the sum of the three distinct areas.

  1. Face areas: 5 × 4 = 20, 5 × 3 = 15 and 4 × 3 = 12 cm².
  2. Each appears twice.
  3. Surface area = 2 × (20 + 15 + 12).
  4. = 2 × 47 = 94 cm².

Final answer. 94 cm²

Interpretation. Counting the pairs prevents the commonest error of missing a face.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.3
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.3

Surface area of pyramids and cones

Inquiry question

How does a slant height differ from a perpendicular height, and which one does each formula use?

Your task

Build a cone and a square-based pyramid from card. For each, measure the slant height and the perpendicular height, and check the relation between them using Pythagoras' theorem. Then compute the surface area from the net.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.3
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.3

Surface area of pyramids and cones

What do you notice?
  • In both solids the slant height was the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle inside the solid.
  • Using the perpendicular height in the curved-area formula would have given the wrong answer.
  • The cone's unrolled sector had radius 5 cm and arc length 2π × 4 cm.
  • The pyramid's four faces were congruent because the base was square.
Observation. The slant height is the height of a face, and it is related to the perpendicular height by Pythagoras' theorem.
Mathematical conclusion

The curved surface area of a cone is πrl and the lateral area of a pyramid is ½ × perimeter × slant height, and in both cases the slant height is the height of a face rather than the height of the solid.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook8.3 · Surface area of pyramids and cones
Chapter 8 · 8.3

Surface area of pyramids and cones

A pyramid has a polygonal base and triangular faces that meet at an apex. The perpendicular height is measured from the apex to the base at right angles; the slant height is measured along a face.

The area of each triangular face is ½ × base × slant height, because the slant height is the height of the triangle in that face.

For a cone, the curved surface unrolls into a sector of a circle of radius l, the slant height, and its area is πrl. The base is a circle of area πr².

Confusing the slant height with the perpendicular height is the standard error. The relation between them is Pythagoras' theorem applied to the right-angled triangle inside the solid.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook8.3 · Worked example 1
Chapter 8 · 8.3 · Worked example 1

Surface area of pyramids and cones

Worked example 8.3.1

Problem. A cone has radius 5 cm and slant height 13 cm. Find its curved surface area and total surface area.

Mathematical reasoning. The curved surface unrolls into a sector of radius l, so its area is πrl, and the base is a circle.

  1. Curved area = πrl = π × 5 × 13 = 65π cm².
  2. Base area = πr² = 25π cm².
  3. Total = 65π + 25π = 90π cm².
  4. = 282.7 cm² to one decimal place.

Final answer. 90π cm², or about 282.7 cm²

Interpretation. The slant height, not the perpendicular height, appears in the curved-area formula because the sector has radius l.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook8.3 · Worked example 2
Chapter 8 · 8.3 · Worked example 2

Surface area of pyramids and cones

Worked example 8.3.2

Problem. A square-based pyramid has base side 8 cm and slant height 10 cm. Find its surface area.

Mathematical reasoning. The base is a square and the four faces are congruent triangles whose height is the slant height.

  1. Base area = 8 × 8 = 64 cm².
  2. Area of one triangular face = ½ × 8 × 10 = 40 cm².
  3. Four faces = 160 cm².
  4. Total = 64 + 160 = 224 cm².

Final answer. 224 cm²

Interpretation. Each face is a triangle, and the slant height is the height of that triangle.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.4
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.4

Volume of prisms and cylinders

Inquiry question

How can the volume of any prism be found from a single cross-section?

Your task

Fill a cylinder with water and pour it into a rectangular tank to find its volume. Then compute the volume from πr²h and compare. Repeat with a triangular prism made from card.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.4
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.4

Volume of prisms and cylinders

What do you notice?
  • The measured and computed volumes agreed to within the precision of the measuring cylinder.
  • The prism rule worked for all three solids.
  • Only the cross-section area changed between the three calculations.
  • The agreement is a check on both the measurement and the formula.
Observation. The volume of a prism is the area of its cross-section times its length, whatever the shape of the cross-section.
Mathematical conclusion

A prism has a constant cross-section and its volume is the area of that cross-section multiplied by the perpendicular length, which covers cylinders as well as polyhedra.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook8.4 · Volume of prisms and cylinders
Chapter 8 · 8.4

Volume of prisms and cylinders

A prism has a constant cross-section parallel to its base. Its volume is the area of that cross-section multiplied by the length perpendicular to it.

This one rule covers cuboids, triangular prisms, cylinders and any other prism, however irregular the cross-section. The cross-section replaces the formula.

A cylinder is a prism with a circular cross-section, so its volume is πr²h.

Volume is measured in cubic units, and the units must be consistent before multiplying. A common error is mixing metres and centimetres.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook8.4 · Worked example 1
Chapter 8 · 8.4 · Worked example 1

Volume of prisms and cylinders

Worked example 8.4.1

Problem. Find the volume of a cylinder of radius 4 cm and height 15 cm.

Mathematical reasoning. A cylinder is a prism with a circular cross-section, so the volume is the cross-section area times the height.

  1. Cross-section area = π × 4² = 16π cm².
  2. Volume = 16π × 15 = 240π cm³.
  3. = 754.0 cm³ to one decimal place.

Final answer. 240π cm³, or about 754.0 cm³

Interpretation. The formula is the prism rule applied to a circular cross-section.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook8.4 · Worked example 2
Chapter 8 · 8.4 · Worked example 2

Volume of prisms and cylinders

Worked example 8.4.2

Problem. A triangular prism has a right-angled triangular cross-section with legs 3 cm and 4 cm, and length 10 cm. Find its volume.

Mathematical reasoning. The volume is the area of the triangular cross-section times the length of the prism.

  1. Cross-section area = ½ × 3 × 4 = 6 cm².
  2. Volume = 6 × 10 = 60 cm³.

Final answer. 60 cm³

Interpretation. The shape of the cross-section does not matter, only its area.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.5
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.5

Pyramids, cones, spheres and composite solids

Inquiry question

Why is the volume of a cone one third of the cylinder that contains it?

Your task

Fill a cone with water and pour it into a cylinder of the same base and height. Record how many fills are needed, then repeat with a pyramid and a prism of the same base and height.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.5
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.5

Pyramids, cones, spheres and composite solids

What do you notice?
  • Exactly three cone fills filled the cylinder, and three pyramid fills filled the prism.
  • The relationship held for a circular base and for a square base.
  • The sphere filled the cylinder one and a half times, which matches the ratio ⁴⁄₃ to 2.
  • The relationship is about the shape, not the size.
Observation. A cone or pyramid has exactly one third of the volume of the prism or cylinder with the same base and height.
Mathematical conclusion

The volume of a pyramid or cone is 13\frac{1}{3}31​ × base area × perpendicular height, which is one third of the containing prism or cylinder.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook8.5 · Pyramids, cones, spheres and composite solids
Chapter 8 · 8.5

Pyramids, cones, spheres and composite solids

A pyramid or cone with the same base and height as a prism or cylinder has exactly one third of its volume. This can be shown by filling a cone three times into the matching cylinder.

The volume of a pyramid or cone is therefore 13\frac{1}{3}31​ × base area × perpendicular height, and for a cone 13\frac{1}{3}31​πr²h.

A sphere of radius r has volume ⁴⁄₃πr³ and surface area 4πr². Both formulas involve the radius cubed and squared respectively, as dimensions require.

A composite solid is handled by splitting it into parts whose volumes can be found, then adding or subtracting. The split is a modelling choice, and it must be stated.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook8.5 · Worked example 1
Chapter 8 · 8.5 · Worked example 1

Pyramids, cones, spheres and composite solids

Worked example 8.5.1

Problem. Find the volume of a cone of radius 6 cm and height 8 cm.

Mathematical reasoning. The cone is one third of the cylinder with the same base and height.

  1. Volume of the matching cylinder = π × 6² × 8 = 288π cm³.
  2. Cone volume = 13\frac{1}{3}31​ × 288π = 96π cm³.
  3. = 301.6 cm³ to one decimal place.

Final answer. 96π cm³, or about 301.6 cm³

Interpretation. The factor of 13\frac{1}{3}31​ is the difference between a cone and a cylinder of the same base and height.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook8.5 · Worked example 2
Chapter 8 · 8.5 · Worked example 2

Pyramids, cones, spheres and composite solids

Worked example 8.5.2

Problem. A sphere of radius 5 cm is placed in a cylindrical tin of radius 5 cm and height 10 cm. Find the volume of the space around it.

Mathematical reasoning. A composite volume is found by subtracting the part that is not wanted from the containing solid.

  1. Tin volume = π × 5² × 10 = 250π cm³.
  2. Sphere volume = ⁴⁄₃π × 5³ = 500π/3 cm³.
  3. Space = 250π − 500π/3 = 250π/3 cm³.
  4. = 261.8 cm³ to one decimal place.

Final answer. 250π/3 cm³, or about 261.8 cm³

Interpretation. The subtraction is legitimate because the sphere sits entirely inside the tin.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.6
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.6

Measurement, density and precision

Inquiry question

How does the precision of a measurement limit the precision of a volume?

Your task

Find the density of an irregular object by measuring its mass and its volume by displacement. Then estimate how the density would change if the volume measurement had a 5% error.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.6
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.6

Measurement, density and precision

What do you notice?
  • The volume came from a difference of two readings, so the errors add.
  • A 2 ml uncertainty in a 58 ml volume is about 3%.
  • The density inherits that uncertainty, so 2.7 g/cm³ is the honest report.
  • The value is close to that of aluminium, which makes the result plausible.
Observation. A volume found by displacement carries the uncertainty of two readings, and the density inherits it.
Mathematical conclusion

Density is mass per unit volume, and because volume is a product of measurements, a small percentage error in each measurement multiplies into the volume and then into the density.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook8.6 · Measurement, density and precision
Chapter 8 · 8.6

Measurement, density and precision

Density is mass per unit volume, so density = mass ÷ volume and volume = mass ÷ density. The units are usually g/cm³ or kg/m³.

Rearranging between mass, volume and density is the same algebraic skill as rearranging any formula, and it is used constantly in materials work.

A volume is a product of three lengths, so a small error in each length is multiplied. A 1% error in a radius gives about a 3% error in a volume.

This is why reported volumes should carry no more significant figures than the measurements support. Extra digits are invented, not measured.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook8.6 · Worked example 1
Chapter 8 · 8.6 · Worked example 1

Measurement, density and precision

Worked example 8.6.1

Problem. A metal block measures 4.0 cm by 3.0 cm by 2.0 cm and has a mass of 190 g. Find its density.

Mathematical reasoning. Density is mass divided by volume, and the volume comes from the three measurements.

  1. Volume = 4.0 × 3.0 × 2.0 = 24 cm³.
  2. Density = 190 ÷ 24 = 7.92 g/cm³.
  3. The measurements have two significant figures, so report 7.9 g/cm³.

Final answer. 7.9 g/cm³

Interpretation. The density suggests the block is made of steel or iron, which is a check on the sense of the answer.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook8.6 · Worked example 2
Chapter 8 · 8.6 · Worked example 2

Measurement, density and precision

Worked example 8.6.2

Problem. A cylinder has radius 5.0 cm and height 12.0 cm. Find its volume and the mass if the material has density 2.7 g/cm³.

Mathematical reasoning. The volume is computed first and then converted to a mass using the density.

  1. Volume = π × 5.0² × 12.0 = 300π cm³ = 942 cm³.
  2. Mass = 942 × 2.7 = 2543 g.
  3. The measurements have two significant figures, so report 2.5 kg.

Final answer. about 2.5 kg

Interpretation. The mass follows from the volume, so it inherits the volume's precision.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookChapter review
Chapter 8 · Review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • A prism has a constant cross-section and volume = cross-section area × length.
  • A cylinder is a prism with a circular cross-section: V = πr²h, curved area = 2πrh.
  • A pyramid or cone has volume 13\frac{1}{3}31​ × base area × perpendicular height.
  • The curved surface area of a cone is πrl, where l is the slant height.
  • A sphere has volume ⁴⁄₃πr³ and surface area 4πr².
  • A composite solid is split into parts whose volumes are added or subtracted.
  • Density = mass ÷ volume.
  • A percentage error in a length multiplies by three in a volume.

Vocabulary

face · edge · vertex · net · cross-section · prism · cylinder · pyramid · cone · sphere · slant height · perpendicular height · composite solid · density · displacement

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookChapter 9 · Bivariate data, correlation and causation
Chapter 9 · Part IV · Data and evidence
09

Bivariate data, correlation and causation

Bivariate data records two measurements of the same subject. A scatter plot shows the association, a line of best fit models it, and the gap between association and cause is where most claims fail.

Engage

A newspaper reports that children who eat breakfast get better exam grades. The data are real and the correlation is real. Does the headline follow from the data?

Framing the inquiry

Key concept: Relationships
Related concepts: Models · Justification
Global context: Fairness and development
Global context exploration: Inequality, difference and inclusion

Statement of inquiry: The relationship between two variables can be modelled by a line of best fit, and the justification required to treat that relationship as causal rather than merely correlated is what separates a mathematical claim from an unsupported one.

Questions to guide us

  • Factual: What is bivariate data, what does a scatter plot show, and how is a line of best fit drawn?
  • Conceptual: Why does a strong correlation not establish causation, and what would be needed to justify a causal claim?
  • Debatable: Should a policy decision be based on a correlation that has no established mechanism?
ATL · Research. In order for a student to evaluate a media claim based on data, students must identify the source and the sample, check whether the measure supports the conclusion, and present the finding with its uncertainty stated.
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.1
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.1

Two variables at once

Inquiry question

How can two measurements of the same subject be recorded and displayed together?

Your task

Collect paired data from your class on two variables of your choice (for example height and hand span, or practice minutes and a game score). Draw a scatter plot, describe the association, and identify any point that does not follow the pattern.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.1
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.1

Two variables at once

What do you notice?
  • The points rise from left to right, so the association is positive.
  • The points lie close to a straight line, so the association is strong.
  • No point was far enough from the pattern to call an outlier.
  • The plot keeps the pairing, so each point is one person.
Observation. A scatter plot keeps the pairing of the two measurements and shows the direction, strength and any exceptions of the association.
Mathematical conclusion

Bivariate data is displayed as a scatter plot with one point per subject, and that plot shows the direction and strength of the association and any point that departs from it.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook9.1 · Two variables at once
Chapter 9 · 9.1

Two variables at once

Bivariate data records two measurements of the same subject: height and weight, study time and score, age and income. Each subject contributes one pair of values.

A scatter plot places one variable on each axis and plots one point per subject. It is the only display that keeps the pairing intact.

A scatter plot shows three things at once: the direction of the association, its strength, and any points that do not follow the pattern.

A point that lies far from the pattern is an outlier. It should be investigated, not deleted, because it may be the most informative point in the data set.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook9.1 · Worked example 1
Chapter 9 · 9.1 · Worked example 1

Two variables at once

Worked example 9.1.1

Problem. Five students record study hours and test scores: (2, 55), (4, 62), (6, 70), (8, 78), (10, 85). Draw a scatter plot and describe the association.

Mathematical reasoning. A scatter plot of paired values shows the direction and strength of the association in one picture.

  1. Label the x-axis with study hours and the y-axis with score.
  2. Plot one point per student.
  3. The points rise from left to right, so the association is positive.
  4. They lie close to a straight line, so the association is strong.

Final answer. a positive, strong, approximately linear association

Interpretation. The plot shows the pattern, but it does not explain it.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook9.1 · Worked example 2
Chapter 9 · 9.1 · Worked example 2

Two variables at once

Worked example 9.1.2

Problem. A data set of height and shoe size contains one point far above the pattern. What should be done with it?

Mathematical reasoning. An outlier may be a recording error or a genuine extreme case, and both are informative.

  1. Check the point against the original record.
  2. If it is a recording error, correct or remove it and say so.
  3. If it is genuine, keep it and note its effect on the line of best fit.
  4. Never delete a point simply because it is inconvenient.

Final answer. investigate the point, then either correct it or keep it and report its effect

Interpretation. Silently removing an outlier changes the conclusion without saying so.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.2
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.2

Measuring linear association

Inquiry question

How can the strength and direction of an association be measured?

Your task

Compute the correlation coefficient for a small data set by hand: find the mean of each variable, compute the products of the deviations, and compare with the product of the standard deviations. Then check your value against a calculator.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.2
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.2

Measuring linear association

What do you notice?
  • The products of the deviations were all positive, which indicates a positive correlation.
  • Their sum was 16, and dividing by the product of the standard deviations gave about 0.99.
  • A calculator gave the same value to two decimal places.
  • The sign of the sum of the products is the sign of the correlation.
Observation. The correlation coefficient is built from the products of the deviations, so its sign records the direction and its size records the strength.
Mathematical conclusion

The correlation coefficient r lies between −1 and 1; its sign gives the direction of the linear association and its magnitude gives the strength, and it says nothing about cause.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook9.2 · Measuring linear association
Chapter 9 · 9.2

Measuring linear association

The direction of an association is positive when both variables rise together and negative when one rises as the other falls.

The strength is measured by how closely the points follow a straight line. The correlation coefficient r takes values from −1 to 1, with the sign giving the direction and the size giving the strength.

A value of r near 0 means no linear association, though a strong curved association is still possible. The coefficient measures linear association only.

Correlation is not causation. Two variables can be strongly correlated because both depend on a third variable, or by coincidence.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook9.2 · Worked example 1
Chapter 9 · 9.2 · Worked example 1

Measuring linear association

Worked example 9.2.1

Problem. Four data sets give r = 0.95, r = −0.82, r = 0.12 and r = −0.05. Describe each association.

Mathematical reasoning. The sign of r gives the direction and its absolute value gives the strength of the linear association.

  1. r = 0.95: positive and very strong.
  2. r = −0.82: negative and strong.
  3. r = 0.12: positive but very weak.
  4. r = −0.05: essentially no linear association.

Final answer. 0.95 very strong positive; −0.82 strong negative; 0.12 very weak positive; −0.05 none

Interpretation. A weak correlation is not a small correlation with the sign removed; it is a different kind of result.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook9.2 · Worked example 2
Chapter 9 · 9.2 · Worked example 2

Measuring linear association

Worked example 9.2.2

Problem. A study finds r = 0.88 between ice-cream sales and drowning deaths. What can and cannot be concluded?

Mathematical reasoning. A high correlation measures association only; causation requires a mechanism or a controlled study.

  1. The correlation is strong and positive.
  2. Both variables rise in summer, so a third variable explains both.
  3. There is no mechanism by which ice-cream sales cause drowning.
  4. So the correlation cannot support a causal claim.

Final answer. a strong positive association exists, but no causal conclusion is justified

Interpretation. The third variable — warm weather — is the explanation for both.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.3
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.3

The line of best fit

Inquiry question

How can a line be drawn through a scatter so that it represents the whole data set?

Your task

Draw a line of best fit for the data (1, 4), (2, 6), (3, 5), (4, 9), (5, 8), (6, 11). Compute the residuals for every point, and adjust your line so that they balance.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.3
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.3

The line of best fit

What do you notice?
  • The residuals were both positive and negative.
  • Their sum was about 1.6, close to zero, so the line was reasonably balanced.
  • The largest residual was 1.5, at x = 4.
  • Moving the line up would make the positive residuals larger and the negative ones smaller.
Observation. A line of best fit is positioned so that the residuals are small and their sum is close to zero.
Mathematical conclusion

A line of best fit passes through the middle of a scatter so that the residuals are small, balanced and patternless, and it is a model of the trend rather than a record of the data.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook9.3 · The line of best fit
Chapter 9 · 9.3

The line of best fit

A line of best fit is a straight line drawn through the middle of a scatter so that the points are balanced on either side and the gaps are as small as possible.

The residuals are the vertical gaps between the points and the line. A good fit has residuals that are small, both positive and negative, and show no pattern.

The line is drawn by eye through the mean point, then adjusted so that the residuals balance. The exact position depends on the method, but any reasonable line gives similar predictions.

The line is a model, not the data. It summarises a trend, and every point that departs from it is information the model does not carry — which is why such models are checked against their residuals before they are used.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook9.3 · Worked example 1
Chapter 9 · 9.3 · Worked example 1

The line of best fit

Worked example 9.3.1

Problem. Draw a line of best fit for the data (1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 6), (4, 8), (5, 9) and find its equation.

Mathematical reasoning. A line through the mean point with a gradient estimated from two well-placed points on the line gives a reasonable fit.

  1. The mean point is (3, 6).
  2. Draw a line through (3, 6) that balances the points.
  3. Two points on the line are (0, 1.6) and (6, 10.4).
  4. Gradient = (10.4 − 1.6)/6 = 1.47, so y = 1.47x + 1.6.

Final answer. y ≈ 1.47x + 1.6

Interpretation. Another student's line will differ slightly, and both are acceptable if the residuals balance.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook9.3 · Worked example 2
Chapter 9 · 9.3 · Worked example 2

The line of best fit

Worked example 9.3.2

Problem. For the line y = 1.5x + 1.5 and the point (4, 8), find the residual.

Mathematical reasoning. A residual is the vertical distance from the point to the line.

  1. Predicted y at x = 4 is 1.5 × 4 + 1.5 = 7.5.
  2. Actual y is 8.
  3. Residual = 8 − 7.5 = 0.5.

Final answer. 0.5

Interpretation. A positive residual means the point lies above the line.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.4
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.4

Correlation, cause and consequence

Inquiry question

When does a correlation justify a causal claim?

Your task

Find three real claims based on correlation: one where a mechanism is plausible, one where a common cause is likely, and one where the direction may be reversed. For each, state which explanation the data can and cannot distinguish.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.4
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.4

Correlation, cause and consequence

What do you notice?
  • Two of the three claims had an obvious common cause.
  • Only the third had a mechanism and controlled-study support.
  • In every case the correlation itself was the same kind of evidence.
  • The difference was in the justification, not in the number.
Observation. A correlation can be explained by A causing B, B causing A, or a common cause, and the data alone cannot distinguish them.
Mathematical conclusion

A causal claim requires a mechanism and evidence from a controlled study; a correlation, however strong, supports only an association.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook9.4 · Correlation, cause and consequence
Chapter 9 · 9.4

Correlation, cause and consequence

A causal claim says that changing one variable produces a change in the other. A correlation only says that the two variables move together.

Three explanations compete whenever a correlation is found: A causes B, B causes A, or a third variable C causes both. A correlation alone cannot distinguish them.

A mechanism is a plausible account of how the cause produces the effect. Without one, a causal claim is a hypothesis rather than a conclusion.

A controlled study, in which the suspected cause is varied while other factors are held constant, is the standard way to test a causal claim. Correlation is not a substitute for it.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook9.4 · Worked example 1
Chapter 9 · 9.4 · Worked example 1

Correlation, cause and consequence

Worked example 9.4.1

Problem. Data show a strong correlation between the number of firefighters at a fire and the damage caused. Should the number of firefighters be reduced to limit damage?

Mathematical reasoning. The third explanation is the correct one, and acting on the correlation would be a mistake.

  1. The correlation is strong and positive.
  2. Firefighters do not cause damage; there is no mechanism.
  3. The size of the fire causes both the number of firefighters and the damage.
  4. So reducing the crew would not reduce the damage.

Final answer. no — the size of the fire is the common cause

Interpretation. This is a case where acting on a correlation would make things worse.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook9.4 · Worked example 2
Chapter 9 · 9.4 · Worked example 2

Correlation, cause and consequence

Worked example 9.4.2

Problem. A trial gives one group a new study method and another group the old method, with students assigned at random. The first group scores higher. What can be concluded?

Mathematical reasoning. Random assignment makes the groups comparable, so a difference in outcome can be attributed to the varied factor.

  1. The groups were assigned at random, so they are comparable.
  2. Only the study method differed.
  3. The outcome differed, so the method is a plausible cause.
  4. The conclusion is a supported causal claim, not merely a correlation.

Final answer. the study method is a supported cause of the higher scores

Interpretation. The support comes from the design of the study, not from the size of the correlation.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.5
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.5

Reading claims critically

Inquiry question

How can a statistical claim be checked before it is believed?

Your task

Take three claims from news or advertising. For each, complete the four checks — source, sample, measure, conclusion — and decide what the data actually support.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.5
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.5

Reading claims critically

What do you notice?
  • Only the third claim stated its sample and its uncertainty.
  • The first claim could not be checked at all.
  • The second claim needed the base rate before it meant anything.
  • The four checks were enough to rank the three claims.
Observation. A statistical claim can be checked by examining its source, its sample, its measure and its conclusion separately.
Mathematical conclusion

A claim is only as strong as the sample that supports it and the measure that expresses it, and the four checks of source, sample, measure and conclusion reveal what the data actually support.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook9.5 · Reading claims critically
Chapter 9 · 9.5

Reading claims critically

A statistical claim rests on four things: the source, the sample, the measure and the conclusion. Each can be checked independently.

The sample must represent the population the claim is about. A sample that is self-selected, small, or drawn from one group cannot support a claim about everyone.

The measure must be the one the conclusion needs. An average hides the spread, and a percentage without a base rate is easy to misread.

A claim that cannot be checked is not necessarily false, but it is not evidence either. Reporting the uncertainty is part of making the claim honestly.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook9.5 · Worked example 1
Chapter 9 · 9.5 · Worked example 1

Reading claims critically

Worked example 9.5.1

Problem. A website reports that 90% of users recommend a product, based on 200 replies out of 50 000 customers. What is wrong with the claim?

Mathematical reasoning. A self-selected sample from a biased source cannot support a claim about the whole population.

  1. The respondents chose to reply, so they are not representative.
  2. 200 of 50 000 is 0.4% of the customers.
  3. The source has an interest in the result.
  4. So the claim is not supported by the evidence given.

Final answer. the sample is self-selected, small and drawn from a biased source

Interpretation. The percentage is arithmetically correct and still does not support the conclusion.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook9.5 · Worked example 2
Chapter 9 · 9.5 · Worked example 2

Reading claims critically

Worked example 9.5.2

Problem. A hospital reports a higher death rate than a neighbouring hospital. What should be checked before concluding that its care is worse?

Mathematical reasoning. A rate comparison is only meaningful when the populations and the definitions are comparable.

  1. Check the case mix: a hospital treating more serious cases will have a higher rate.
  2. Check the base rate: small hospitals have unstable rates.
  3. Check the definitions and the time period.
  4. Only then is a comparison of the two rates meaningful.

Final answer. case mix, base rate, definitions and time period must all be comparable

Interpretation. The same arithmetic on different populations gives different answers.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookChapter review
Chapter 9 · Review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • Bivariate data records two measurements of the same subject.
  • A scatter plot shows direction, strength and outliers.
  • The correlation coefficient r lies between −1 and 1 and measures linear association only.
  • A line of best fit balances the residuals and passes through the mean point.
  • A residual is the vertical gap between a point and the line.
  • Interpolation is inside the range of the data; extrapolation is outside it.
  • A causal claim needs a mechanism and a controlled study.
  • A claim is checked through its source, sample, measure and conclusion.

Vocabulary

bivariate data · scatter plot · association · correlation coefficient · line of best fit · residual · outlier · interpolation · extrapolation · causation · common cause · base rate · sample · population

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookChapter 10 · Probability, sampling and evidence
Chapter 10 · Part IV · Data and evidence
10

Probability, sampling and evidence

Probability is a number between 0 and 1 that measures uncertainty. It is built from a model of the outcomes, and the model must be stated before the number means anything.

Engage

A medical test for a rare condition is 99% accurate. A patient tests positive. How likely is it that the patient actually has the condition? The answer surprises most people, and the reason is a base rate.

Framing the inquiry

Key concept: Logic
Related concepts: Quantity · Models
Global context: Identities and relationships
Global context exploration: Beliefs and values

Statement of inquiry: The logic of probability, and the models built from it, allow a quantity of uncertainty to be assigned to an event, and that quantity is what allows a decision to be justified rather than guessed.

Questions to guide us

  • Factual: How is the probability of an event calculated, and what are the addition and multiplication rules?
  • Conceptual: Why does the probability of a combined event depend on whether the events are independent, and how does a base rate change the interpretation of a test result?
  • Debatable: Should a decision about a person be made on a probability alone?
ATL · Communication. In order for a student to explain a probabilistic result to an audience, students must state the model used, express the result as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage, and say plainly what the number does and does not mean.
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.1
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.1

Outcomes, events and probability

Inquiry question

How can the likelihood of an event be assigned a number?

Your task

Roll two dice 60 times and record the total each time. Compute the experimental probability of each total, then compare with the theoretical probabilities from the sample space of 36 outcomes.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.1
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.1

Outcomes, events and probability

What do you notice?
  • The experimental probabilities were close to the theoretical ones.
  • No total appeared exactly as often as the theory predicts.
  • The most likely total, 7, was also the most frequent in the experiment.
  • The differences would shrink with more rolls.
Observation. Experimental probabilities approach theoretical probabilities as the number of trials increases, but they do not match exactly in a small sample.
Mathematical conclusion

P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total equally likely outcomes, and the experimental probability estimates it with an error that shrinks as the number of trials grows.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook10.1 · Outcomes, events and probability
Chapter 10 · 10.1

Outcomes, events and probability

The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes of an experiment. An event is a subset of the sample space, and the probability of an event measures how much of the sample space it covers.

When all outcomes are equally likely, P(event) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of outcomes. This is the definition, and it depends on the assumption of equal likelihood.

Probabilities lie between 0 and 1, and the probabilities of all outcomes sum to 1. The complement rule P(not A) = 1 − P(A) follows directly.

The model is a choice. A fair die has six equally likely outcomes; a loaded one does not, and no calculation can detect that. The model must be stated and justified.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook10.1 · Worked example 1
Chapter 10 · 10.1 · Worked example 1

Outcomes, events and probability

Worked example 10.1.1

Problem. Two fair dice are thrown. Find the probability that the total is 7.

Mathematical reasoning. There are 36 equally likely outcomes, and six of them give a total of 7.

  1. The sample space has 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes.
  2. The pairs giving 7 are (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1): six of them.
  3. P(total is 7) = 6/36 = 1/6.

Final answer. 1/6

Interpretation. The assumption of equal likelihood is what makes the count of outcomes enough.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook10.1 · Worked example 2
Chapter 10 · 10.1 · Worked example 2

Outcomes, events and probability

Worked example 10.1.2

Problem. A bag holds 3 red and 5 blue counters. Find P(red), P(not red) and P(red or blue).

Mathematical reasoning. The sample space has eight equally likely outcomes, and the events are subsets of it.

  1. Total counters = 8.
  2. P(red) = 3/8.
  3. P(not red) = 1 − 3/8 = 5/8.
  4. P(red or blue) = 1, because every counter is one or the other.

Final answer. P(red) = 3/8, P(not red) = 5/8, P(red or blue) = 1

Interpretation. The complement rule is faster than counting the blue counters, and it gives the same answer.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.2
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.2

Compound events: tables, trees and Venn diagrams

Inquiry question

How can the probability of a combination of events be found?

Your task

Toss two fair coins 80 times. Record whether the results are the same or different, then compute the experimental probabilities. Compare with the theoretical probabilities from a tree diagram, and repeat with a spinner divided into three equal sectors.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.2
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.2

Compound events: tables, trees and Venn diagrams

What do you notice?
  • The experimental probabilities were close to the theoretical ones.
  • 'One of each' was the most likely outcome, as the theory predicts.
  • The two orderings, head then tail and tail then head, are separate outcomes.
  • Combining them gives P(the same) = 1/2.
Observation. The probabilities of combined outcomes follow from multiplying along the branches of a tree and adding across the branches that belong to the event.
Mathematical conclusion

For independent events P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B), for mutually exclusive events P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B), and the general rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B) covers every case.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook10.2 · Compound events: tables, trees and Venn diagrams
Chapter 10 · 10.2

Compound events: tables, trees and Venn diagrams

Two events are independent when the outcome of one does not affect the other. For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

Two events are mutually exclusive when they cannot both happen. For mutually exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).

The general addition rule is P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B), and the subtraction removes the outcomes counted twice.

Sample-space diagrams, tree diagrams and Venn diagrams are three representations of the same logic. The tree makes independence visible; the Venn diagram makes the overlap visible.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook10.2 · Worked example 1
Chapter 10 · 10.2 · Worked example 1

Compound events: tables, trees and Venn diagrams

Worked example 10.2.1

Problem. A fair coin is tossed and a fair die is rolled. Find P(head and 6).

Mathematical reasoning. The two events are independent, so their probabilities multiply.

  1. P(head) = 1/2 and P(6) = 1/6.
  2. The events are independent, so multiply.
  3. P(head and 6) = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12.

Final answer. 1/12

Interpretation. The tree diagram shows twelve equally likely combined outcomes, one of which is head and 6.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook10.2 · Worked example 2
Chapter 10 · 10.2 · Worked example 2

Compound events: tables, trees and Venn diagrams

Worked example 10.2.2

Problem. A card is drawn from a standard pack. Find P(heart or king).

Mathematical reasoning. The general addition rule removes the card that is both a heart and a king, which would otherwise be counted twice.

  1. P(heart) = 13/52 and P(king) = 4/52.
  2. P(heart and king) = 1/52.
  3. P(heart or king) = 13/52 + 4/52 − 1/52 = 16/52.
  4. = 4/13.

Final answer. 4/13

Interpretation. The Venn diagram shows the overlap that the subtraction removes.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.3
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.3

From theory to experiment

Inquiry question

How does an experimental probability compare with a theoretical one?

Your task

Roll a die 120 times and record the frequency of each face. Compute the experimental probability of each face, compare with 1/6, and decide whether the die behaves fairly. Then pool your results with two other groups.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.3
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.3

From theory to experiment

What do you notice?
  • All six frequencies were close to 20, which is 1/6 of 120.
  • The largest difference was 0.017, which is small.
  • Pooling three groups gave 360 rolls and even closer agreement.
  • The evidence supports a fair die, but does not prove it.
Observation. Experimental probabilities from a large number of trials agree closely with the theoretical value, and pooling trials improves the agreement.
Mathematical conclusion

An experimental probability estimates the theoretical probability, and a large difference between them is evidence that the model is wrong rather than that the calculation failed.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook10.3 · From theory to experiment
Chapter 10 · 10.3

From theory to experiment

An experimental probability is a relative frequency: the number of times an event occurred divided by the number of trials. It is an estimate, not a definition.

The theoretical probability comes from a model of the outcomes. When the model is correct, the experimental probability approaches it as the number of trials grows.

A large difference between the two is evidence that the model is wrong, not that the mathematics failed. A die that never shows 6 in 60 rolls is probably loaded.

A small difference is expected. The question is always whether the difference is small enough to be explained by chance, which is the beginning of formal statistical testing.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook10.3 · Worked example 1
Chapter 10 · 10.3 · Worked example 1

From theory to experiment

Worked example 10.3.1

Problem. A spinner is divided into four equal sectors. In 200 spins it lands on red 46 times. Estimate P(red) and compare with the theoretical value.

Mathematical reasoning. The experimental probability is a relative frequency and estimates the theoretical value.

  1. Experimental P(red) = 46/200 = 0.23.
  2. Theoretical P(red) = 1/4 = 0.25.
  3. The difference is 0.02, which is small.
  4. So the model of four equal sectors is plausible.

Final answer. 0.23 experimentally, against 0.25 theoretically

Interpretation. The small difference is what we expect from a fair spinner, and it does not overturn the model.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook10.3 · Worked example 2
Chapter 10 · 10.3 · Worked example 2

From theory to experiment

Worked example 10.3.2

Problem. A coin is tossed 100 times and gives 68 heads. Is the coin fair?

Mathematical reasoning. A large departure from the theoretical value is evidence against the model.

  1. Experimental P(head) = 68/100 = 0.68.
  2. Theoretical P(head) for a fair coin = 0.5.
  3. The difference of 0.18 is large for 100 tosses.
  4. So there is evidence that the coin is not fair.

Final answer. the coin is probably not fair

Interpretation. The conclusion is about the model, and it is stated as evidence rather than proof.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.4
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.4

Populations, samples and bias

Inquiry question

How can a sample be chosen so that it represents a population?

Your task

Estimate the proportion of students in the school who walk to school, using three samples: the first 20 people you meet, 20 people chosen at random from a list, and everyone in one class. Compare the three estimates.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.4
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.4

Populations, samples and bias

What do you notice?
  • The convenience sample gave the highest estimate, because it met people arriving on foot.
  • The class sample was not representative of the whole school.
  • The two random samples agreed with each other.
  • Doubling the random sample changed the estimate only slightly.
Observation. A random sample gives an estimate that does not depend on how the sample was reached, and a larger random sample reduces the variability.
Mathematical conclusion

A sample represents a population only when selection is random, and bias from a non-random selection is not reduced by increasing the sample size.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook10.4 · Populations, samples and bias
Chapter 10 · 10.4

Populations, samples and bias

A population is the whole group a claim is about, and a sample is the part that is measured. A parameter describes the population and a statistic describes the sample.

A sample is representative when every member of the population has a known, non-zero chance of being selected. Convenience and self-selected samples fail this test.

Bias is a systematic error in the selection. It cannot be reduced by taking a larger sample, because a bigger biased sample is still biased.

A random sample removes selection bias, and a larger sample reduces the variability of the estimate. The two effects are different and both matter.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook10.4 · Worked example 1
Chapter 10 · 10.4 · Worked example 1

Populations, samples and bias

Worked example 10.4.1

Problem. A school of 1 200 students is surveyed by asking the first 40 students who arrive. Explain why the sample is biased.

Mathematical reasoning. Students who arrive early differ systematically from those who arrive late, so the sample is not representative.

  1. The population is all 1 200 students.
  2. The sample is the first 40 arrivals, chosen by convenience.
  3. Early arrivals are likely to differ from the rest in ways that matter.
  4. So the estimate is biased, and taking 400 instead of 40 would not fix it.

Final answer. the sample is a convenience sample and is biased

Interpretation. Bias is about how the sample was chosen, not how big it is.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook10.4 · Worked example 2
Chapter 10 · 10.4 · Worked example 2

Populations, samples and bias

Worked example 10.4.2

Problem. Explain the difference between a population parameter and a sample statistic.

Mathematical reasoning. The parameter is fixed but unknown, and the statistic varies from sample to sample.

  1. The parameter describes the whole population and cannot usually be computed.
  2. The statistic is computed from the sample and varies between samples.
  3. The statistic is used as an estimate of the parameter.
  4. The quality of the estimate depends on the sampling method.

Final answer. a parameter describes the population; a statistic describes the sample

Interpretation. Confusing the two is what allows a biased sample to be reported as a fact about everyone.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.5
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.5

Risk, base rates and decisions

Inquiry question

How should a probability be interpreted when a decision must be made?

Your task

Model a screening test for a condition with a base rate you choose. Build a table for 10 000 people, compute the true and false positives, and find the posterior probability. Then change the base rate and repeat.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.5
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.5

Risk, base rates and decisions

What do you notice?
  • The posterior probability rose steadily with the base rate.
  • The number of false positives fell as the base rate rose, even though the test's accuracy never changed.
  • At a 1% base rate, more than nine in ten positive results were false.
  • At a 50% base rate, nine in ten positive results were correct.
Observation. The probability that a positive result is correct depends far more on the base rate than on the accuracy of the test.
Mathematical conclusion

A probability must be interpreted against its base rate, because a rare event produces mostly false positives even with an accurate test — and a decision must weigh the consequences as well as the number.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook10.5 · Risk, base rates and decisions
Chapter 10 · 10.5

Risk, base rates and decisions

The base rate is the frequency of an event in the whole population, before any test or indicator is applied. It is the starting point for interpreting a test result.

A test with high accuracy can still give mostly false positives when the condition is rare, because the number of healthy people is far larger than the number of affected people.

The posterior probability is found by comparing the true positives with the total positives, and it depends on the base rate as much as on the accuracy.

A decision based on a probability must also weigh the consequences. The same probability can justify different actions when the costs of being wrong differ.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook10.5 · Worked example 1
Chapter 10 · 10.5 · Worked example 1

Risk, base rates and decisions

Worked example 10.5.1

Problem. A condition affects 1 in 1 000 people. A test is 99% accurate. A patient tests positive. Find the probability that the patient has the condition.

Mathematical reasoning. The posterior probability compares the true positives with all positives, and it is dominated by the base rate.

  1. Of 100 000 people, 100 have the condition and 99 900 do not.
  2. True positives ≈ 0.99 × 100 = 99.
  3. False positives ≈ 0.01 × 99 900 = 999.
  4. P(condition given positive) = 99/(99 + 999) ≈ 0.09.

Final answer. about 9%

Interpretation. A 99% accurate test still gives mostly false positives when the condition is rare, because the base rate is tiny.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebook10.5 · Worked example 2
Chapter 10 · 10.5 · Worked example 2

Risk, base rates and decisions

Worked example 10.5.2

Problem. A screening programme for a condition affecting 1 in 20 people uses a test that is 95% accurate. Find the probability that a positive result is correct.

Mathematical reasoning. The same calculation with a different base rate gives a very different answer.

  1. Of 1 000 people, 50 have the condition and 950 do not.
  2. True positives ≈ 0.95 × 50 = 47.5.
  3. False positives ≈ 0.05 × 950 = 47.5.
  4. P(condition given positive) = 47.5/95 ≈ 0.5.

Final answer. about 50%

Interpretation. The test is only slightly less accurate, but the base rate is fifty times higher, so the result is far more informative.

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookChapter review
Chapter 10 · Review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total equally likely outcomes.
  • Probabilities lie between 0 and 1 and sum to 1 over the sample space.
  • P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
  • For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
  • P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
  • An experimental probability estimates the theoretical probability.
  • A representative sample requires random selection; bias is not fixed by size.
  • A posterior probability depends on the base rate as much as on the accuracy.

Vocabulary

sample space · outcome · event · equally likely · complement · independent · mutually exclusive · tree diagram · Venn diagram · experimental probability · theoretical probability · population · sample · bias · base rate · posterior probability

MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookFormula bank

Formula bank (1 of 6)

Key facts and formulas, chapter by chapter. Use them to check work, not to replace reasoning.

The real number system

Rational number
any number that can be written as a/b with integers a, b and b ≠\neq= 0; its decimal either terminates or recurs.
Irrational number
a number that cannot be written as a fraction; its decimal neither terminates nor recurs.
Surd
an exact irrational root, such as √2 or 3√5.
Absolute value
|x| is the distance of x from 0 on a number line.
Interval notation
[a, b] includes both ends; (a, b) excludes both; [a, b) includes a only.
Set notation
A ∪\cup∪ B is the union, A ∩\cap∩ B the intersection, A′\prime′ the complement.
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookFormula bank

Formula bank (2 of 6)

Key facts and formulas, chapter by chapter. Use them to check work, not to replace reasoning.

Powers, roots and notation

Product law
am^{m}m × an^{n}n = am+n^{m+n}m+n.
Quotient law
am^{m}m ÷ an^{n}n = am−n^{m-n}m−n for a ≠\neq= 0.
Power law
(am^{m}m)n^{n}n = amn^{mn}mn.
Zero and negative indices
a⁰ = 1 for a ≠\neq= 0; a−n^{-n}−n = 1/an^{n}n.
Rational index
a^(1/n) is the nth root of a; a^(m/n) = (n^{n}n√a)m^{m}m.
Scientific notation
a × 10n^{n}n with 1 ≤ a < 10.
Significant figures
the digits that carry measured meaning, counted from the first non-zero digit.
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookFormula bank

Formula bank (3 of 6)

Key facts and formulas, chapter by chapter. Use them to check work, not to replace reasoning.

Algebra and functions

Function
a rule that gives exactly one output for each input in its domain.
Domain and range
the set of permitted inputs and the set of resulting outputs.
Expanding
a(b + c) = ab + ac.
Difference of squares
a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b).
Perfect square
a² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)².
Rearranging a formula
apply the same inverse operation to both sides to isolate the wanted letter.
nth term
a linear sequence has term = mn + c; a quadratic sequence has constant second difference.
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookFormula bank

Formula bank (4 of 6)

Key facts and formulas, chapter by chapter. Use them to check work, not to replace reasoning.

Linear models and systems

Straight line
y = mx + c, where m is the gradient and c the y-intercept.
Gradient
m = (y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁), the change in y per unit change in x.
Direct proportion
y = kx, a straight line through the origin.
Simultaneous equations
solve by substitution or elimination; check in both equations.
Inequality
multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign.
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookFormula bank

Formula bank (5 of 6)

Key facts and formulas, chapter by chapter. Use them to check work, not to replace reasoning.

Shape, space and trigonometry

Congruence
SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS for triangles.
Similarity
corresponding angles equal and corresponding sides in the same ratio.
Pythagoras
a² + b² = c² for the hypotenuse c of a right-angled triangle.
Trigonometric ratios
sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite/adjacent.
Angles of elevation and depression
measured from the horizontal, and equal by alternate angles.
Prism
volume = area of cross-section × length; surface area is the sum of the face areas.
Cylinder
volume = πr²h; curved surface area = 2πrh; total surface area = 2πrh + 2πr².
Pyramid
volume = 13\frac{1}{3}31​ × base area × perpendicular height.
Cone
volume = 13\frac{1}{3}31​πr²h; curved surface area = πrl, where l is the slant height.
Sphere
volume = ⁴⁄₃πr³; surface area = 4πr².
Density
density = mass ÷ volume.
MYP Mathematics 3 · Student coursebookFormula bank

Formula bank (6 of 6)

Key facts and formulas, chapter by chapter. Use them to check work, not to replace reasoning.

Data, probability and evidence

Bivariate data
paired measurements of two variables for the same subject.
Correlation
the strength and direction of a linear association, measured by r with −1 ≤ r ≤ 1.
Line of best fit
a line drawn through the middle of a scatter so that the residuals are balanced.
Interpolation and extrapolation
predicting inside or outside the range of the collected data.
Causation
correlation alone never establishes cause; a mechanism or a controlled study is required.
Probability of an event
P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total equally likely outcomes.
Compound events
P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) for independent events; P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
Sample and population
a sample estimates a population parameter; bias makes the estimate unreliable.
Base rate
the underlying frequency of an event in the whole population, needed to interpret a test result.

MYP Mathematics · Student coursebookSecond edition
About this book

Ten chapters that take the real number system, powers and notation, functions, linear models, systems, transformations, similarity, trigonometry, three-dimensional measurement, bivariate data and probability from first ideas to justified use. Each chapter opens with a task: you investigate, notice a pattern, state a mathematical conclusion you can defend, and only then meet the formal explanation — with worked examples that model a complete solution and practice separated into Criterion A, B, C and D sets so you can see which skill each task trains.

Year 3 reasoning is organised, not just correct: Criterion C tasks ask you to structure an argument, and Criterion B tasks ask you to justify a generalisation rather than to list cases. Every chapter closes with a reflection that returns to the statement of inquiry.

Every chapter also closes with a Service as Action opportunity, a Community Project connection and a Personal Project extension for MYP 5. The back of the book carries complete student-facing answers with reasoning, a formula bank, a glossary and references.
